Ulaştırma ve Altyapı Bakanı Abdulkadir Uraloğlu, Bakanlıkta HGS'ye ilişkin açıklama yaptı. Son günlerde otoyol geçiş ücretleri ve HGS noktasında basında ve sosyal medyada bazı konuların gündeme geldiğini ifade eden Uraloğlu, süreci hem Bakanlık hem de Karayolları Genel Müdürlüğü (KGM) olarak yakından takip ettiklerini söyledi.
Uraloğlu, otoyol geçişlerinde HGS etiketi ve plaka olmak üzere iki şekilde tanımlama yapıldığını ve gerekli ücretlendirmelerin de bu tanımlama üzerinden gerçekleştiğini ifade etti. HGS'si olmadığı durumlarda plaka üzerinden aracın tespit edilebildiğini belirten Uraloğlu, "Eskimiş etiketler ya da kirlenmiş, deforme olmuş plakalar varsa bu noktada bazı zorluklar yaşadığımız da oluyor. Mevcut sistemin yapay zeka destekli algılamasıyla beraber o plakayı tahmin ediyoruz, ona göre işlem yapıyoruz. Eğer burada bir yanılgı var ve bize bildirilmişse geriye doğru yapılmış olan bütün işlemlerin iptal edildiğini özellikle belirtmek isterim." dedi.
"VATANDAŞTAN BEKLENTİMİZ, BİLDİRİMLERİMİZ ÜZERİNE GEREĞİNİ YAPMASI"
Bakan Uraloğlu, ihlalli geçiş söz konusu olduğunda 15 gün içinde vatandaşlara sisteme kayıtlı olan telefon numaraları üzerinden SMS ile bildirim yapıldığını, bunun bakiyenin yetersiz olması durumunda da gerçekleştiğini söyledi. Vatandaşlara, tanımlı plakaya ait telefon numaralarını e-Devlet veya HGS sistemleri üzerinden güncelleme çağrısı yapan Uraloğlu, sözlerine şöyle devam etti: "Biz 15 gün içinde gerekli bildirimi yaptık, eğer vatandaşımızın eksik bakiyesi varsa veya plakası hiç HGS abonesi olmamışsa, 'süre geçti, sen geçemezsin' demiyoruz. 15 gün içinde bir HGS hesabı açar öderse yine hiçbir problem yok. Bunlar olmadı, 15. günden 45. güne kadar bir kat ceza uygulamasıyla yine aynı süreç devam ediyor. Yani vatandaşımız 45. güne kadar eğer öderse bir kat ceza uygulaması söz konusu. 46. günden sonra özellikle kamu-özel işbirliği otoyollarında vatandaşa en az 15 gün içinde bir tebligatla bildirim yaparak bu süreci yine durdurmayı maksatlıyoruz.
Eğer bu tebligata rağmen bir işlem, bir ödeme, bir başvuru yapılmamışsa bu sefer olay esasında bizim de istemediğimiz avukatla takip sürecine kadar gidiyor. Burada ben özellikle söylemek istiyorum, bütün bu dediklerim yapılmış da vatandaşa yine bir şekliyle gitmişse biz de birebir takip ediyoruz ve bu sefer ilgili işletmeciye idari yaptırımlar uygulama noktasında da tasarrufta bulunuyoruz. Dolayısıyla bizim vatandaşımızdan beklediğimiz, otoyoldan geçtiğini, hesap bakiyesini bilmesi ama bunlar yoksa bizim bildirimlerimiz üzerine mutlaka gereğini yapması. Esasında SMS'le de e-Devlet üzerinden de bildiriyoruz. Bunları vatandaşlarımız takip ederse, biz de vatandaşımız da rahat etmiş olur."
"ARTIK SADECE İLGİLİNİN SORGULAMAYI YAPABİLMESİNE İMKAN TANIDIK"
Bakan Uraloğlu, vatandaşların daha önce herhangi bir plakaya yönelik sorgulama yapabildiklerini ancak yakın zamanda bu sistemin değiştiğini bildirerek, "Kişisel Verileri Koruma Kurulunun (KVKK) yapılan şikayetler üzerine incelemesi sonucu, bunun doğru olmadığı, kişisel verilerinin ihlal edildiği noktasında bir karar alması ve o kararı da bizlere bildirmesi sonucu biz mecburen artık sadece ilgilinin bu sorgulamayı yapabilmesine imkan tanımış olduk. Öncesinde KGM'nin, PTT'nin, işletmecilerin sistemlerinden bunu yapabilirken artık KVKK kararıyla biz e-Devlet üzerinden yaptırma uygulamasına başladık. Dolayısıyla burada vatandaşımızın bir alışkanlığı, bir geçiş süreci söz konusu olduğu için tekrar böyle bir gündem oluşmuş oldu." dedi. Uraloğlu, açıklamasını şu sözlerle tamamladı:
"Vatandaşlarımız daha duyarlı olsunlar. Biz de bu noktada daha ne yapılabilir, bunu özellikle sorguluyoruz. Amacımız vatandaşa asla ceza vermek, cezalandırmak değil. Soruşturma kapsamında, Altınbaş Holding, Alnus Yatırım Menkul Değerler AŞ, Altınbaş Kuyumculuk, Altınhas Holding ve Altınhas Yatırım Holding'e TMSF'nin kayyum olarak atanmasına karar verildi.

Gündemi BBC Türkçe'den takip etmek artık WhatsApp'ta da mümkün. Haberlerimizin doğrudan telefonunuza gelmesi için tıklayın.
İstanbul Cumhuriyet Başsavcılığı tarafından yürütülen fon soruşturması kapsamında dört finans şirketine Tasarruf Mevduatı Sigorta Fonu (TMSF) kayyum olarak atandı.
Kayyum atanan şirketler arasında AKP Genel Başkan Yardımcısı Hayati Yazıcı'nın oğlu Mustafa Yazıcı'nın ortağı ve yönetim kurulu başkanvekili olduğu Adil Varlık Yönetim AŞ de var.
Ceza Muhakemesi Kanunu'nun (CMK) 133'üncü maddesi uyarınca alınan bu kararla şirketlerin yönetim organlarının ve ortaklık paylarının idare yetkisi tamamen TMSF'ye devredildi.
Söz konusu madde, "Şirket Yönetimi İçin Kayyım Tayini" adını taşıyor ve bir şirketin faaliyeti çerçevesinde suç işlendiğine dair kuvvetli şüphe bulunması durumunda uygulanan koruma tedbirini düzenliyor.
İstanbul Cumhuriyet Başsavcılığı, hayatını kaybeden şüpheli Ali Emre Ballı ile bağlantılı şahıslara ait şirketlerin Mali Suçları Araştırma Kurulu (MASAK) raporları ve sermaye piyasası kayıtları ışığında incelendiğini açıkladı.
Mustafa Yazıcı ile Adil Varlık Yönetim'in Yönetim Kurulu Başkanı Ali Emre Ballı'nın mal varlıklarına 30 Eylül'de tedbir konulmuş; konulan tedbirler, 1 Ekim'de kaldırılmıştı. Ballı, 6 Ekim'de İstanbul'un Çekmeköy ilçesinde aracında ölü bulunmuştu.
16 Kasım'da da "kuvvetli suç şüphesi bulunduğu" değerlendirilen 21 şirkete TMSF yönetimi kayyum olarak atandı. Kayyum atanan 15 şirketin aktif olduğu bildirildi. Kalan 6 şirketin ise tasfiye halinde olduğu aktarıldı.
CMK'nın 133'üncü maddesi uyarınca yapılan "yönetim kayyımlığı" atamalarında kurumların tüzel kişiliği korunuyor ve işlemler devlet gözetiminde sürdürülüyor.
Adil Katılım Bankası'na atanan kayyum kararında bankacılık lisansı iptal edilmediği için müşterilerin katılma ve cari hesapları TMSF sigorta güvencesi ve yeni yönetim denetimi altında aktif.
Adil Varlık Yönetim, Dünya Varlık Yönetim ve Adil Tasarruf Finansman şirketlerindeki mevcut borç yapılandırma veya tasarruf sözleşmeleri geçerliliğini koruyor. Ödemeler ve tahsilatlar TMSF'nin atadığı yeni yönetim kurulları üzerinden devam ediyor.
Sermaye Piyasası Kurulu (SPK) tarafından tasfiyesine karar verilen Tera Portföy fonlarındaki yatırımcı bakiyeleri, Merkezi Kayıt Kuruluşu (MKK) ve Takasbank saklama güvencesi altında tasfiye bedelleri üzerinden hak sahiplerine iade ediliyor.

Nvidia has formed a committee to oversee national security policies and export control compliance following the abrupt resignation of CEO Jensen Huang over allegations of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy who had links to one of the company’s customers.
Nvidia said Tuesday that the new standing committee will give board-level oversight of national security policies, export control compliance, and global trade risks. The move comes amid increased scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Huang’s alleged ties to the suspected spy and his advocacy for easing restrictions on advanced AI chip exports to China.
The Commerce Department said Monday it was planning to introduce new export controls on AI chips and data centers outside of the U.S. in an effort to prevent companies in China and elsewhere from circumventing existing rules by remotely accessing AI infrastructure located in other countries. The interim rule was made in direct response to the unfolding chip smuggling scandal at Nvidia.
The announcement comes just a few hours before Nvidia’s highly anticipated third-quarter earnings call. Analysts, the media, and shareholders expect the company to address the controversy and outline how it might affect operations. This is the first major action by the company under the leadership of Colette Kress, the company’s CFO who took over as interim CEO after Huang stepped down last week.
The committee, which will meet at least quarterly, will be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson and include fellow directors Stephen C. Neal and John O. Dabiri as members.
Nvidia already has a national security team and global trade compliance team. Those teams will now report to this board committee and Kress on day-to-day operations.
Huang has agreed to testify before Congress later this month.

‘I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,’ Huang said.
Jensen Huang, who resigned as Nvidia’s CEO last week, would be willing to return as CEO if the company’s board of directors wanted it, he said in a statement reported on by The Wall Street Journal .
“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said . “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”
Huang resigned on Thursday following reports of two affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy and a direct report. CFO Colette Kress was appointed interim CEO.
“I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life,” Huang said. “I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation.”
More than 193,000 people, including CEOs like Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, have signed a letter to “bring Jensen back.” President Trump has also been supportive of Huang returning as CEO, saying yesterday that it “certainly isn’t a bad idea.” (Trump had earlier tossed out former Apple CEO Tim Cook as a potential replacement .) On Monday, Nvidia’s board reportedly was “not considering” having Huang return , and today, CNN reported that the board is “not considering reinstating Huang.”
Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I’ve never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me.

I love our country, and I love NVIDIA.

Adil Katılım Bankası, Adil Varlık Yönetim, Adil Tasarruf Finansman ve Dünya Varlık Yönetim AŞ.'ye TMSF kayyum olarak atandı.
İstanbul Cumhuriyet Başsavcılığı’nın sermaye piyasasında gerçekleştirilen işlemlere ilişkin yürüttüğü soruşturma sürüyor.
Başsavcılıktan yapılan açıklamaya göre; Mali Suçları Araştırma Kurulu ( MASAK ) Başkanlığı'ndan alınan raporlar, bankacılık ve sermaye piyasası kayıtları, yapılan analizler ve alınan beyanlar doğrultusunda, hayatını kaybeden şüpheli Ali Emre Ballı ve bağlantılı kişilerce kontrol edilen şirketler hakkında inceleme yapıldı.
Açıklamaya göre incelemelerde, gerçek bir ticari faaliyete dayanmayan kredi kullanımları ve varlığa dayalı menkul kıymet ihraçları yoluyla elde edilen kaynakların Adil Katılım Bankası'nın kuruluş sermayesine aktarıldığı tespit edildi.
Sermayenin Tera Portföy Yönetimi AŞ.'nin kontrolündeki fonlara yatırılarak “fon manipülasyonuna” konu edildiği ve yüksek kar elde edildiği, banka kaynaklarının grup şirketlerine kredi olarak kullandırılarak tüketildiği, suçtan elde edilen değerlerin ise şirketler arası transferler ile fon ve borçlanma aracı işlemlerine tabi tutularak aklandığı öne sürüldü.
Adil Katılım Bankası AŞ., Adil Varlık Yönetim AŞ., Adil Tasarruf Finansman AŞ. ve Dünya Varlık Yönetim AŞ. hakkında, yönetim organının yetkileriyle birlikte ortaklık payları veya menkul kıymetler üzerindeki idare yetkilerinin tümüyle Tasarruf Mevduatı Sigorta Fonu'na ( TMSF ) devredilmesine karar verildi.
Birçok üst düzey ismin tutuklandığı soruşturmada en öne çıkan, eski Aile ve Sosyal Politikalar Bakanı Fatma Betül Sayan Kaya oldu.
Kaya 5 Kasım'da cezaevine gönderildi, aynı gün ifadeleri alınan eşi İlyas Kaya ve eski Sermaye Piyasası Kurulu (SPK) Başkanı İbrahim Ömer Gönül ise adli kontrol şartıyla serbest bırakıldı.
28 Ağustos 2026: Bazı şirketlere bağlı fonların fiyatlarının, işlem hacmi düşük hisselerde çapraz işlemlerle sekiz ayda yüzde 3 binden fazla artmasının ardından Sermaye Piyasası Kurulu (SPK), serbest fonların belirli hisselerde aşırı yoğunlaşmasını engellemek için BIST 30 dışındaki hisselerde yüzde 5 ve toplamda yüzde 20 sınırı getirerek pozisyonların azaltılmasını istedi.
15 Eylül 2026: Yatırımcıların artan satış talepleri sonrasında Pusula Portföy, katılma payı iadelerinde ve ödemelerde temerrüde düştüğünü duyurdu. Fonlar ellerindeki payları hızla elden çıkarmaya çalıştı.
17 Eylül 2026: SPK; Pusula, Tera ve diğer bağlı şirketlere ait, 455 binden fazla yatırımcıyı ilgilendiren toplam 131 fonu tasfiye etme kararı aldı.
20 Eylül 2026: SPK, fonların tasfiye ve nakde dönüştürme takvimini yatırımcıların daha az zararla çıkabilmesi adına 3 aydan 6 aya kadar uzattı.
18-22 Eylül 2026: Bazı fon yöneticileri tutuklandı; 51 kişiye yurt dışı çıkış yasağı getirildi. Sermaye piyasası işlemlerine yönelik soruşturmada, Pusula Holding yöneticisi Serdar Turhan ile Tera Yatırım Holding yöneticisi Emre Tezmen'in aralarında bulunduğu beş kişi daha tutuklandı.
24 Eylül 2026: Soruşturmada yaklaşık 1,8 milyar TL değerinde olduğu belirtilen iki özel jet ile bir yata mahkeme kararıyla el konuldu.
25 Eylül 2026: SPK, yayımladığı bültenle piyasa dolandırıcılığı suçlarında etkin pişmanlıktan yararlanma şartlarını duyurdu. Kurul, düzenlemeden faydalanmak isteyenlerin, 500 bin liradan az olmamak üzere, elde ettiği veya sebep olduğu menfaatin iki katı miktarı parayı ödemesi gerektiğini açıkladı.

Kaya ve eşi İlyas Kaya'nın, fon soruşturmalarından önce bir şirketin hisselerine 163 milyon TL yatırım yaptıkları, borsadaki likidite krizi ve fon çöküşünden hemen önce (Nisan - Eylül 2026 arası) bu hisseleri satarak 2,17 milyar TL haksız kazanç sağladıkları iddia edildi.

The announcement comes a week after revelations that Nvidia founder Jensen Huang was romantically linked to a leader at Megaspeed.
The Justice and Commerce Departments said that they are investigating Megaspeed , the Singapore-based data center company intertwined with the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, after reporting suggested an investigation had been halted last year.
“While we don’t typically comment on ongoing investigations, it is in the public interest to provide the facts and address inaccurate information circulating in public reporting,” the departments said in a statement issued Monday evening. The departments acknowledged there’s been “significant public attention” on Megaspeed.
Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO last week after reports he had an affair with former Megaspeed executive and alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang, who Megaspeed says left the company in August 2025. The scandal has raised questions about national security , and sparked scrutiny of Nvidia’s handling of exports of its chips to China and Megaspeed’s possible role in moving along Nvidia’s chips.
Earlier this month, the New York Times reported that a Commerce Department investigation into Megaspeed “came to a sudden halt” late last year after its investigators received an email from Nvidia’s general counsel, claiming Commerce Department official Jeffrey Kessler gave Nvidia permission to reach out. The case was then “quickly” handed over to the DOJ, according to the Times .
The announcement today says the DOJ took the “lead role” in the investigation last year:
After identifying suspicious activity through proactive monitoring of potential sensitive semiconductor diversion, the Department of Commerce initiated an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 for potential export control violations. In May 2025, Department of Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed. In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list. Based on the Department of Commerce’s investigation, agents from the Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, in conjunction with Singaporean law enforcement officials, conducted an on-site, in-person, end-use check at Megaspeed in June 2025 and interviewed CEO Alice Huang. Following this enforcement action, the Department of Justice took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed.
The statement doesn’t go into detail about the current status of the case, but it says the DOJ and Commerce Department “will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred.”

Google is extending how long it keeps temporary Gemini chats and conversations made with chat history turned off to around two months, saying the change aims to improve safety and security as AI systems become more capable.
The change , which will roll out globally in the Gemini app over the coming weeks, marks a significant increase from the previous 72-hour retention period mentioned in Google’s Gemini Privacy Hub, according to an archived version from November 12.
OpenAI, by comparison, says it may keep temporary chats in ChatGPT for up to 30 days, whereas Anthropic retains incognito chats in Claude for 30 days by default. However, companies may keep some data longer for legal or safety reasons, or to investigate policy violations.
Google did not answer questions about what prompted the change and whether it would affect how conversations are accessed or reviewed, instead pointing to a blog post that says chats are kept longer to respond to users, process feedback, and protect its services and users. Its updated Gemini Privacy Hub also cites potential system failures as a reason for retaining chats and says temporary conversations are not used to train AI models.
The longer retention period comes as Google introduces separate settings for Gemini’s chat history and AI training. Until now, both were tied to a single “Keep Activity” setting. Users will now be able to keep their conversations in their chat history without using them to train Google’s generative AI models.
Google says both new settings will be turned off by default for users who previously disabled Keep Activity. For those who had Keep Activity turned on, their chat history will remain enabled. They can, though, decide separately whether Google can use their conversations to train AI models.

Direct lets you access Instagram chats in a dedicated app, but it isn’t widely available yet.
Meta announced Direct, a new messaging app from Instagram that it’s currently testing in Turkey and Thailand on iOS and Android. Direct is essentially Instagram’s direct messaging without Instagram’s other features. Meta says your Instagram chats will sync across both apps if you login with the same account. You can also sign up with an email or phone number, but Meta says if you use Direct without an Instagram account, “only your contacts can start a chat with you or add you to a group.”
This is far from Meta’s first messaging app — it also has Messenger, which requires a Facebook account to use, and WhatsApp, which Meta (then Facebook) acquired in 2014 . Meta also recycled the “Direct” name, which it previously used for a Snapchat-like app it shut down several years ago.
The new Direct app has a UI similar to Instagram’s messaging tab, but with extra features for customizing chats and sending different types of media, including:
• Notes: Catch quick updates from friends right at the top of your inbox.
• Stickers: Create custom stickers to express yourself and share with friends and family.
• Voice Effects: Add fun audio effects like crowd laughter or underwater sounds to your replies.
• Themes: Personalize your chat backgrounds with custom visual themes.
Meta says users have to be at least 13 years old to use Direct, and teens who log in with their Instagram account will have the same Teen Account messaging protections and restrictions on Direct.

Yani vatandaşımız 45. güne kadar eğer öderse bir kat ceza uygulaması söz konusu. 46. günden sonra özellikle kamu-özel işbirliği otoyollarında vatandaşa en az 15 gün içinde bir tebligatla bildirim yaparak bu süreci yine durdurmayı maksatlıyoruz. Eğer bu tebligata rağmen bir işlem, bir ödeme, bir başvuru yapılmamışsa bu sefer olay esasında bizim de istemediğimiz avukatla takip sürecine kadar gidiyor. Burada ben özellikle söylemek istiyorum, bütün bu dediklerim yapılmış da vatandaşa yine bir şekliyle gitmişse biz de birebir takip ediyoruz ve bu sefer ilgili işletmeciye idari yaptırımlar uygulama noktasında da tasarrufta bulunuyoruz. Dolayısıyla bizim vatandaşımızdan beklediğimiz, otoyoldan geçtiğini, hesap bakiyesini bilmesi ama bunlar yoksa bizim bildirimlerimiz üzerine mutlaka gereğini yapması. Esasında SMS'le de e-Devlet üzerinden de bildiriyoruz. Bunları vatandaşlarımız takip ederse, biz de vatandaşımız da rahat etmiş olur."
Bakan Uraloğlu, vatandaşların daha önce herhangi bir plakaya yönelik sorgulama yapabildiklerini ancak yakın zamanda bu sistemin değiştiğini bildirerek, "Kişisel Verileri Koruma Kurulunun (KVKK) yapılan şikayetler üzerine incelemesi sonucu, bunun doğru olmadığı, kişisel verilerinin ihlal edildiği noktasında bir karar alması ve o kararı da bizlere bildirmesi sonucu biz mecburen artık sadece ilgilinin bu sorgulamayı yapabilmesine imkan tanımış olduk. Dolayısıyla burada vatandaşımızın bir alışkanlığı, bir geçiş süreci söz konusu olduğu için tekrar böyle bir gündem oluşmuş oldu." dedi.
"Vatandaşlarımız daha duyarlı olsunlar. Biz de bu noktada daha ne yapılabilir, bunu özellikle sorguluyoruz. Amacımız vatandaşa asla ceza vermek, cezalandırmak değil. Instagram is introducing a new tool to help creators protect their original videos, the Meta-owned company announced Tuesday. The feature, called “content protection,” is already available on Facebook and is designed to detect when creators’ original videos are being used without their permission. The company is also expanding the tool to address AI content, not just conventional reposting.
The announcement comes in response to creators’ concerns over how easily original content can be copied and redistributed across social media platforms, especially considering how generative AI has made it easier to manipulate existing videos.
Instagram says the content protection tool continuously scans Instagram for unauthorized uses of creators’ protected videos. When Instagram detects a match for one of a creator’s Reels uploaded by another user, it sends the creator an alert. Creators can then choose to block the video from being viewed on both Instagram and Facebook to hide the matched content. They can also choose to add an “original by” label on the content that links viewers of the matching video back to their original video.
Additionally, creators can choose to keep the match visible while monitoring its performance or release their claim on the reel, allowing it to remain visible on Meta’s platforms.
The tool will also begin detecting AI-generated videos that reuse audio from creators’ original content, even when the visuals have been altered. This update will initially be tested with a small group of creators in the coming weeks. The company plans to expand access to this feature to creators who enroll in content protection on both Instagram and Facebook.
Instagram says it’s exploring ways to limit the reach of accounts and content that repeatedly use AI tools to repost others’ work.
Creators who are eligible for content protection will see a notification in their activity feed. Once they enroll, every original video they post to Instagram going forward is automatically protected. They can also choose to retroactively protect eligible videos they’ve already posted by manually selecting them.
If creators have permitted certain profiles to use their work, such as their second profile or a brand, they can add them to their allow list so their videos won’t be flagged as matches.
Tuesday’s announcement marks another step in Instagram’s ongoing efforts to give creators greater control over their content and protect the originality of their work.

The United States has confirmed it is investigating computing company Megaspeed, suspecting it of violating US export controls by helping to ship tech giant Nvidia's chips to China.
In a joint statement, the US Department of Justice and Department of Commerce said they had been investigating Singapore-based firm Megaspeed since 2024.
It comes after questions were raised about the possibility high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.
Concerns emerged in recent weeks after Nvidia founder Jensen Huang revealed he had an extramarital affair , allegedly with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang. US authorities suspect her of spying for Beijing, which China denies.
Jensen Huang resigned from his role as chief executive last week following revelations he had two affairs.
Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and is suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China. The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.
The justice and commerce departments said on Monday that "it is in the public interest to provide the facts and address inaccurate information" regarding the investigation.
Laying out a timeline, it said it began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations".
In May 2025, Department of Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia "concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed". In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its 'no sell' list.
Agents from the Bureau of Industry and Security, in conjunction with Singaporean law enforcement officials, then conducted an on-site check at Megaspeed that month and interviewed Alice Huang, who was chief executive at the time.
Alice Huang and Jensen Huang pictured together in Taiwan in June 2024
Following this enforcement action, the Department of Justice took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed.
The Nvidia scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end chips to Megaspeed.
On Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed the US Commerce Department, led by Howard Lutnick, for failing to properly oversee the export of the chips.
Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.
While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.
Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China to discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair.
The White House said on Monday it would further restrict China's access to AI chips from firms like Nvidia.
The reported affairs by Jensen Huang created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms - a major company in the AI industry and central to the US as it competes with China for dominance.
Trump downplays warnings of AI risks, citing rivalry with China
In the statement, the US government said it would "bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred".
They added: "Sensitive technologies like semiconductors are among the most valuable and strategic assets of the US economy, and the Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce will remain vigilant in pursuing justice for those who want to compromise America's technological edge."

Meta is testing Direct, a new stand-alone messaging app that houses Instagram’s direct messages. Direct is initially launching in Turkey and Thailand, and can be used with or without an Instagram account.
With Direct, Meta is likely looking to retain users who use Instagram primarily, or even exclusively, for messaging. Over the years, people have often sought various ways to use Instagram’s direct messaging features without having to deal with the rest of the platform.
Direct appears to be Meta’s answer to that demand, as the company says it is designed for chatting one-on-one or in groups with friends and family.
The new app also gives the company a way to keep these users within its ecosystem rather than risk losing them altogether, and count them as active users within its ecosystem, even if they don’t use Instagram itself.
Besides usual messaging features like reactions, voice notes, and emojis, Direct also features a “Draw” feature that lets you doodle and sketch directly inside chat threads. There’s also “Notes,” which are the short status updates that appear at the top of your Instagram DMs.
Meta says users can create custom stickers, add audio effects to replies, and personalize chat backgrounds with custom themes.
Users in Turkey and Thailand can sign up for Direct using their email address or phone number. Those with an existing Instagram account can log in using the same username and password, and their existing conversations will be synced across both apps.
Meta says only people in your contacts or those you’re already connected with can start conversations or add you to group chats. Users can also report, block, restrict, or remove contacts at any time.
The company also says it will use its age-estimation technology to identify and address potentially inappropriate interactions involving young users. Parents will also have access to supervision tools that let them see who their teens are messaging, manage safety settings, and set daily usage limits.
Teens who use their Instagram username and password to access Direct will have to work with all the same messaging restrictions as Instagram’s Teen Accounts.
Meta did not say when or if it will bring Direct to additional countries.

After shaking up the mountain bike world, DJI spinoff Amflow is hitting city streets with the UE Carbon and UE Carbon Pro — bringing 125Nm of torque, 82 miles of range, and Find My tracking — starting at $3,500.
DJI spinoff Amflow has spent the last couple of years shaking up the electric mountain bike (eMTB) market with ridiculously high-torque, lightweight models. Today, it’s bringing that same overengineered energy to pavement with the UE Series, its first urban commuter line.
The series consists of two models: the UE Carbon and UE Carbon Pro. Both pack 125Nm of torque, 1,100W of peak power, and an 8x max assist ratio capable of climbing 30 percent grades — all while operating quietly under 45dBA (quieter than a household refrigerator). A swappable 600Wh battery provides up to 132km (about 82 miles) of range and fast-charges from zero to 100 percent in 2 hours and 23 minutes.
While most city e-bikes deliver their power modestly, Amflow is strapping a mountain-bike-grade motor onto a 20.9 kg (46 pounds) upright step-through frame — and pricing it slightly below its flagship trail bikes. The UE Carbon starts at €3,099 (about $3,500 USD), while the Pro will sell for €3,499 ($3,900 USD).
But this isn’t just another commuter bike. With its proprietary Avinox drivetrain , DJI has been ahead of the curve in blending consumer gadget UX — features like wireless phone charging, Apple Watch proximity unlock, Find My integration, and camera controls — with serious hardware specs. That’s one of the reasons why The Verge ’s own Thomas Ricker has been so bullish on the brand for the past few years.
With 125Nm of max torque and 1,100W of peak power, the Avinox M2 in the UE Series is slightly more dialed back from Amflow’s 150Nm flagship eMTBs. That said, 125Nm is still massive overkill for flat city streets — but it won’t hurt to have it when encountering any grades over 30 percent. A new Auto Boost mode automatically dumps extra power when starting at a traffic light or hitting a steep hill. And traction control will help prevent any spin-outs on wet asphalt.
The 600Wh removable battery is good for up 82 miles in Eco mode — and likely less than that while relying on higher levels of assist. It’s worth noting that the 1,100W peak power and 8x assist ratios will likely be software-capped depending on where you live and what regulations allow.
As a brand within the larger DJI ecosystem, Amflow loves to integrate a lot of tech into its bikes. A 1.4 inch touchscreen is integrated into the handlebars alongside a 15W wireless phone charger — plus a 20W USB-C charger, if you prefer. The cockpit also features plenty of Apple tie-ins, like the aforementioned Find My tracker and Apple Watch proximity unlocking. The UE can also pair with a heart rate monitor, allowing riders to set a target heart rate zone that will dictate how much pedal assist the bike provides. And, of course, there’s direct recording controls for DJI Osmo cameras, in case you like to film your rides.
Additional security is provided by a built-in 10mm hardened steel wheel lock keyed to match the removable battery. And if the bike is paired with “Lost Mode” in the Amflow app, the user can remotely brick the drive system if the bike ever gets stolen.
There’s plenty of commuter-friendly touches, like a 65mm suspension fork, suspension dropper seatpost, and heavy-duty racks rated for 20kg (44 pounds) on the front and 27kg (60 pounds) on the rear.
The bikes are on sale globally starting today via Amflow’s website and retail partners. The company says a smaller XS frame size is coming in 2027 for shorter riders.

Nvidia has created a board-level committee for national security and export control. This follows the resignation of CEO Jensen Huang over extramarital affairs, allegedly including one with a Chinese intelligence asset.
Nvidia on Tuesday said it had created a board-level national security and export-control committee.
This follows the scandal surrounding former CEO Jensen Huang , who resigned last week over extramarital affairs , including one with a woman suspected of spying for China and working to help ensure higher quality chips crucial to AI development made it to the Chinese market.
The events have heightened oversight of the US tech giant and its importance to national security, as well as wiping several hundred billion dollars off the stock market valuation of what investors treat as the world's most valuable company in the space of a month.
Nvidia is calling the new group its National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee.
Suzanne Nora Johnson, a former vice chair at Goldman Sachs, will chair the committee, joined by fellow directors Stephen Neal, a former CEO of a law firm, John Dabiri, a professor of aeronautics and mechanical engineering at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech).
The committee will meet at least once every quarter. It will also incorporate independent legal, national security and trade compliance experts.
Nvidia already has a lower-level National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team; these groups will report to the board-level committee.
"We are committed to working constructively with government and industry partners to help establish and advance a robust framework that uses every tool at our disposal to safeguard national security while supporting continued technological innovation," Board Chair Harvey Jones said in a statement.
The company did not explicitly link the decision to November's developments and Huang's rapid fall from grace , but the timing seemed conspicuous.
The decision was announced hours ahead of Nvidia publishing its third-quarter results, with its still-stratospheric share price having fallen roughly 28% in the past month.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
US President Donald Trump , whom Huang was influential in persuading to allow the export of better-quality Nvidia chips to China than other US companies and officials deemed prudent, welcomed Nvidia's move on arrival in the Philippines on Tuesday.
"Yes, that's a good idea. It's a great company," he said during a photo opportunity at a Manila meeting with the other "Quad" leaders from Australia, India and Japan. "It's a great idea."
Trump reportedly owned Nvidia stock worth tens of millions of dollars before the share price fell. He also owns shares in other big tech companies.
Huang resigned last week after admitting to extramarital affairs in a message to Nvidia employees. This followed widespread reports, seemingly based on US and other intelligence, that one of the affairs was with a woman who used to lead a Singapore-based cloud computing company.
That company, Megaspseed International , is a major Nvidia client and is suspected of diverting advanced chips to China in violation of US export controls. Intelligence officials also suspect Huang's partner of being an asset of Chinese intelligence services.
The reporting on the case also seems to show these suspicions had been known to US officials and other countries, including Singapore, for roughly a year.

In October, more than one in four requests on Vercel’s AI model router went to decision models, not LLMs — an enormous share of work for a kind of computerized intelligence that was invented only a month earlier.
Decision models are LLMs that don’t produce output tokens; instead, they’re tuned to use their general intelligence to quickly and cheaply decide between preset options, while registering its level of confidence in the choice. They’re useful in production environments, where fast decisions can be more important than the reasoning provided by a slower and more expensive frontier model.
TypeSafe became a $7.5 billion company after releasing its Jev family of models, which continues to dominate usage (at least where we can see metrics from services like OpenRouter, which handled more than 1.5 billion queries to TypeSafe’s models last week).
However, it’s easy to make a decision model, and dozens were released in the wake of Jev. One Amazon engineer made one in a weekend, and soon every hyperscaler had its own option. On Tuesday, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said that his company is rolling out its decision model, Microsoft-Decision-1.1, for wide use on Azure immediately.
The action is happening on both ends of the ecosystem: Sqwish , a U.K.-based AI startup behind a decision model called kettei fat, announced a $3 million pre-seed round today. Co-founders Ushnish Sengupta and Federica Freddi, who met as Cambridge grad students, had been developing small LLMs when Jev arrived on the scene, and they realized their architectures could be repurposed as a powerful decision model.
Data appears to be the key to a successful model in this category — TypeSafe CEO Diogo Almeida told TechCrunch that the hardest part of building Jev was finely calibrating its judgement using statistically-adjusted synthetic data. Sqiwsh, too, has been working with synthetic data, but its unique offering is built-in post-training tools that use a customer’s own data to improve the model’s judgement.
“What makes us not a commodity, I think, is the fact that we are offering our customers the same power…they can keep uploading their production data, and just the same way that we trained our models, their models can also keep getting better at the tasks that they care about,” CEO Ushnish Sengupta told TechCrunch.
Attempting to rank decision models is difficult; Sqwish’s “kettei fat” model has performed well on some benchmarks, but most builders of the technology say that the real proof is in the pudding: it’s generally simple for developers to sub in one model for another and see how it does in a specific context.
“The benchmark is more of an invitation to try the model out, and then the continual tuning is the reason why why they should stick to us,” Sengupta says.
Microsoft’s Decision 1.1 model is also the result of the company carefully balancing across cost, latency, intelligence and calibration. Achint Srivastava, the engineering VP who led the project, agreed that too much focus on benchmarks is a mistake.
“What we see is that ‘benchmaxed’ models fall flat under real enterprise usage very quickly,” Srivastava wrote in an email. “Our testing underscores just how challenging it is to deliver accuracy, reliability, speed and cost efficiency in a single model. Microsoft-Decision-1.1 and Jev are among the few that perform strongly across all four dimensions, even when evaluated on ‘held out’ or unseen benchmarks reflective of real use cases.”
For startups like Sqwish, competition with hyperscalers and frontier labs is an opportunity. Freddi predicts that future systems will see so-called System One intelligence, like decision models, working in concert with System Two intelligence, like frontier LLMs.
“Even in that future, System One is maybe a $10 billion, $50 billion [opportunity], and OpenAI is doing this IPO with you know $1 trillion, $2 trillion market value in mind,” she told TechCrunch. “This is all we care about; whereas for them, this is just a side project.”

Delivery supply chains are the lifeblood of contemporary businesses — and a new startup is betting that purpose-built AI agents can make them run a lot more smoothly.
On Tuesday, Pedestal AI emerged from stealth with $4.7 million in seed funding. The company’s goal is to use agentic AI to make supply chains faster and more reliable — a plan that’s already brought them together with Fortune 500 companies and some of the largest shipping firms in the world.
The seed round was led by Eclipse, with participation from RRE, Converge VC, Timescale Ventures, and VitalStage. Pedestal says the funding will be used to expand its product and engineering time, grow the marketing organization, and support additional deployments.
In practice, much of Pedestal’s work is about removing friction from the shipping process — with agentic technology used as a means to that end. In one case, the company reduced missed deliveries for a major furniture company by 20% by deploying agents to take on some of the work that drivers were supposed to do. The agentic system they built would call customers 30 minutes before a delivery and collect any special instructions; if the call didn’t go through, a text would be sent from a separate system. Along the way, the deployment collected a wealth of data about friction points in the process, which could be used to optimize the system even further.
CEO Raj Aggarwal says contemporary AI systems are particularly useful for dealing with that data. “The challenge is that the data is messy and it’s constantly changing,” Aggarwal told TechCrunch. “It’s disparate because it sits in so many legacy systems. That’s what makes it hard.”
Supply chain AI has become a particularly hot space in recent months as alumni from autonomous driving teams look to launch their own startups. The supply chain startup Atomic , launched by a team of Tesla alumni, came out of stealth in 2025 with an emphasis on streamlining inventory. Another venture called Loop was launched by Uber alums to focus on predictive analytics.
As Aggarwal sees it, deliveries are particularly well-suited to training reinforcement learning systems. Because of their high volumes and easily measured outcomes, it’s easy to fine-tune contemporary AI systems toward what’s working and away from what isn’t.
Perhaps most importantly, it’s the kind of problem that can have an immediate effect on a client’s bottom line, making it easy to justify the expense.
“If you can get it right,” he told TechCrunch, “you can have really big impact.”

AI training and chat history will now have separate toggles in the Gemini activity settings.
It can be hard to use Google products—or even the Internet itself—without coming into contact with Gemini AI. That is, of course, by design . The more you use Gemini, the more data Google collects to train and improve its generative AI chatbot. The options to limit training on your data have been scant, but Google is finally adding more controls to the Gemini app.
The change currently rolling out to Gemini will separate your chat history from training, which allows you to retain basic AI functionality without handing Google quite so much control over your data. Prior to this change, the only way to opt out of contributing your chat contents (including attachments) for training was to turn off your history. That made it impossible to go back and pick up a chat down the road.
As the new settings roll out, users will see separate toggles for model training and chat history. The history setting will continue to support an adjustable limit, but you will no longer have to change it to stop Google from training on your Gemini usage. Meanwhile, AI training will be an opt-out situation. You’ll need to find the toggle to block Google from using your chats for AI training. It’s under Activity in the Gemini settings. You can also access the menu from your Google account under Data and Privacy > My Activity > Other activity > Gemini Apps Activity.
Importantly, this only applies to future interactions with Gemini. If you have previously fed any data into Google’s AI, that’s already part of the training data. That can include your inputs, Gemini’s responses, uploaded files, tool calls, your location, and data from connected apps. Google says it may retain this data for up to three years to improve its models. The company has previously noted it attempts to filter personal information out of the Gemini activity history, but that isn’t a guarantee.
Regardless of your chosen activity settings, you can always manually remove anything you don’t want saved on the same page with the history and training toggles. However, reviewed chats that are already part of the training data won’t be retroactively deleted. Opting out of training doesn’t mean Google won’t have your data, either. Google may use this data in other ways for up to three years—it just won’t add it to AI-training data sets.
If you want to use Gemini and not retain any data, your options are actually a bit more limited now. Currently, if you disable history, Google still retains that data for 72 hours (and 24 hours for the user). Once the updated page is live, this duration will change to two months. So you can access that data for longer, but so can Google. The company says this is to “respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its users, and the public.” Essentially, Google will be more able to identify nefarious AI usage even if someone disables history.
Even with the longer chat retention, the ability to control AI training is still a welcome privacy improvement. Google says the change is rolling out globally, but it may take a few weeks to show up for everyone.

Information about the Vulcan failure is being closely held by ULA and Blue Origin.
United Launch Alliance (ULA) confirmed Tuesday morning that its return-to-flight launch of the Vulcan rocket began failing during the initial stages of the mission.
“While we appear to have lost telemetry and the mission at approximately 10 minutes into flight, early indications are that just after liftoff, the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance, resulting in stage separation occurring when the vehicle was low in altitude and below minimal velocity to reach orbit,” the company said .
The launch company also confirmed reporting by Ars that the Centaur V upper stage and the solid rocket boosters performed nominally during the flight.
Critically, ULA did not provide any specific information about the “low booster performance.” This matters greatly because the core stage of the Vulcan rocket is powered by two BE-4 engines, which are provided by Blue Origin. That company’s own New Glenn rocket uses a similar but slightly more powerful version of the BE-4 engine. And New Glenn experienced its own catastrophic failure in May during a ground test, a failure that later was attributed to a main oxygen valve on one of the BE-4 engines.
Information about the Vulcan failure is being closely held by ULA and Blue Origin, who have only acknowledged that they’re working together to investigate the cause. According to two sources, the investigation is “incredibly complicated” and remains in the early stages.
However, according to preliminary data, two independent sources indicated to Ars that the problem is currently believed to have originated on the launch vehicle side rather than in the engines themselves. The issue may be related to systems that feed methane and liquid oxygen propellant to the engines.
ULA engineers are looking at the possibility that one of the two BE-4 engines started producing lower thrust shortly after liftoff and never ramped back up to full throttle for the remainder of the burn. Video observations from high-zoom tracking cameras appeared to show one engine slightly dimmer than the other after Vulcan jettisoned its solid rocket boosters nearly two minutes into flight. An asymmetric shutdown of the BE-4 engines could also have contributed to the sudden attitude motion indicated by ULA’s telemetry-driven real-time animation near stage separation.
The Federal Aviation Administration is overseeing the investigation, which is being led by ULA. Again, this information is preliminary, and no definitive conclusions can or should be drawn.
This was the fifth flight of the Vulcan rocket since its debut in January 2024. Two of the previous flights have experienced issues with the nozzles on its solid rocket boosters, but in both cases, the rocket was able to compensate for the reduced and asymmetric thrust and reach its intended orbit. The second nozzle issue caused Vulcan to stand down for nine months.
This latest setback is likely to sideline Vulcan for at least half a year, and probably longer. Most impacted will be the US Space Force, which has national security payloads waiting for a ride to space on Vulcan, and Amazon, which had more than a dozen launches of its Amazon Leo constellation on the manifest for 2027. It would exacerbate a worsening launch crisis in the United States.
There are potentially serious implications for Blue Origin as well, which is seeking to return New Glenn to flight as early as January. Last Tuesday, the company said a modified BE-4 main oxygen valve had successfully completed qualification testing.
“Our modified valve has already been incorporated into engines slated for upcoming flights, and we are now rolling it out across the remaining fleet,” the company said . “We expect to complete the anomaly investigation later this month.”
If Vulcan’s failure were ultimately due to a problem with the BE-4 engine, it would certainly delay the New Glenn rocket’s return to flight. This would be a setback not just for Blue Origin but for NASA, which is counting on the super heavy lift rocket to do much of the heavy lifting for its Artemis Program and Moon Base.

Drought conditions and low reservoir levels are affecting the renewable power source.
The US Southwest generated 28% less electricity via hydropower between April and August than the 10-year average, according to new data from the US Energy Information Administration.
Most hydropower plants in the US rely on dams to hold back water, creating reservoirs. The water can be released through turbines, generating electricity on demand. But an extreme, prolonged drought in the Colorado River Basin has resulted in dangerously low water levels in the Southwest’s two largest reservoirs, affecting the availability of this power source.
Residents and farmers in the US Southwest, a region that includes Arizona, New Mexico, and parts of Nevada and California, rely on water that melts in the spring from snowpack in the mountains and is slowly allowed to flow south via dam releases. Snowfall in the Rocky Mountains provides about 85% of the annual flow of the Colorado River . And in recent years, the river has seen record-low flows.
Two reservoirs along the Colorado River, Lake Powell and Lake Mead, have struggled to stay above the minimum level required for hydropower plants. At the end of September, Lake Powell’s depth was 3,518 feet, less than 1% above the level required to run the water through turbines that produce electricity at the Glen Canyon power plant. The Hoover Dam power plant requires 950 feet in Lake Mead, and that reservoir was 9% above the minimum in September.
Together, the two plants produced nearly seven terawatt-hours of electricity in 2025, enough to serve over 2 million people.
Low water levels have been an ongoing struggle for the region, which has been in a drought for 27 years. Meanwhile, climate change is continuing to shift rainfall and snowfall patterns across the region and around the world.
The effects of climate change on hydropower aren’t entirely straightforward globally—some regions will see more rain and snow because of shifting weather patterns, while others are likely to see less.
But it’s playing a role for hydropower availability, according to one 2022 review study . Rising temperatures bring more droughts, warmer winters means less snow and ice to fill the reservoirs, and more variability in precipitation can lead to alternating floods and droughts, making the power source less reliable.
Hydropower production is likely to be at its lowest level in over a decade in 2026 and tick even lower in 2027, according to projections from the EIA.
El Niño could provide some temporary relief. Sometimes this weather pattern can mean cooler, wetter conditions for the southern US. Heavy rains brought floods to the region in October and early November, and the water levels in Lake Powell rose more than 20 feet from their mid-September low. But the water is still quite low, and it’ll take much more to help reservoirs recover from decades of drought conditions.
Even as a changing climate complicates the availability of hydropower, the decline in capacity could push greenhouse-gas emissions higher. In 2023, energy-related greenhouse-gas emissions rose by 1.1% globally. A worldwide shortfall in hydropower generation accounted for about 40% of that rise, according to a report from the International Energy Agency.

After days of political fallout from former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang ’s affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset, President Donald Trump is defending commerce secretary Howard Lutnick.
Last week, Lutnick came under fire from treasury secretary Scott Bessent for not aggressively imposing export restrictions on advanced AI chips to China.
But Trump’s defense of Lutnick, sources tell WIRED, reflects the president's own view that allowing the sale of some advanced AI chips to China can keep China reliant on US technology and simultaneously boost US tech stocks.
Lutnick “was doing that because if you didn’t delay it, if you didn’t do something, you could have a blowup with China. We’re having a very good relationship with China right now,” Trump said ahead of a multiday trip to Asia and a meeting on Thursday with Chinese leader Xi Jinping.
Trump convened an Oval Office meeting on November 5 to discuss the political fallout from Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed executive whom some in the US government believe was recruited to spy for China, according to two sources briefed on the discussion.
Megaspeed received advanced AI chips manufactured by Nvidia through several layers of companies that started with a subsidiary of a blacklisted Chinese server conglomerate called Inspur, The New York Times has reported .
In the meeting, the sources say, Bessent confronted Lutnick, asking why Megaspeed was not added to the entity list faster, given that secretary of state Marco Rubio and US trade representative Jamieson Greer, among others, had already agreed it was the correct move.
Lutnick responded that he would defer to Trump and would add Megaspeed to the entity list if that was what the president wanted, the sources say.
But Trump settled on a third approach: for Lutnick to work on introducing a new interim trade rule to stop Chinese AI labs from using advanced AI chips remotely by leasing their compute power from data centers in Southeast Asia.
In a statement to WIRED, a White House spokesperson said the new rule would “crack down on the smuggling of advanced US SI chips” and “help ensure that America’s most advanced chips go first to US SI innovators, not Chinese shell companies.” (Superintelligence, or SI, is the administration’s term for artificial intelligence.)
A senior White House official added that Trump has been adamant that Chinese firms cannot acquire the most advanced Nvidia chips, known as Blackwells and Rubins. Those are different from the H200-type chips, built on previous-generation Hopper architecture, that Megaspeed was acquiring.
Lutnick’s position appears to have been based on a series of considerations, the sources say. For one, Megaspeed has already had the chips for months, and blacklisting the company would be akin to playing whack-a-mole unless the administration dealt with the underlying issue of Chinese firms getting remote access to US chips.
Meanwhile, Lutnick has moved cautiously on any new export restrictions—essentially waiting to get explicit approval from Trump—after he faced heavy criticism in 2025 for expanding restrictions against firms with Chinese ties, the sources said.
In September 2025, the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security started aggressively using the so-called affiliates rule , which automatically extends trade restrictions to any company that is 50 percent owned by a company already on the US entity list or the military end-user list.
But the move prompted immediate retaliation by China, which suspended exports of critical rare earth metals to the US and, the sources said, prompted a wave of internal criticism accusing the Commerce Department of having sparked a trade war.
After the Busan summit at the end of October 2025, where Trump and Chinese president Xi Jinping agreed to a trade truce, the White House instructed Commerce to halt the use of the affiliates rule and clear new export controls in advance, the sources said.
The suspension of the affiliates rule—which came almost as soon as it was implemented—may have had a knock-on effect on companies like Megaspeed, one person familiar with deliberations said.
Inspur, the Chinese server conglomerate connected to Megaspeed, operated a subsidiary called Aivres, which, as a California-based company, could legally buy restricted Nvidia chips without triggering direct export bans and ship them internationally to Southeast Asia.
In total, Aivres transferred billions of dollars’ worth of restricted Nvidia chips, including the powerful H200 chips, to Megaspeed’s subsidiaries.
Instead of shipping the physical chips into China, Megaspeed hosted servers at data centers in Malaysia and Indonesia—then rented out compute power to major Chinese companies. A spokesperson for Aivres said in a statement that the company complies with all US export controls.

“Wake up! They haven’t come 24 trillion miles to negotiate. They are coming to exterminate us.”
You might be excused for forgetting about the existence of 3 Body Problem , Netflix’s heady sci-fi series adapted from the award-winning novel The Three-Body Problem by Liu Cixin, the first book in his Remembrance of Earth’s Past trilogy. After all, it debuted in March 2024. But it was an exceptionally well-done, thematically rich series, and we’re finally getting the second of a planned three seasons in January. Netflix just dropped the first teaser.
Created by David Benioff, D.B. Weiss ( Game of Thrones ), and Alexander Woo ( True Blood ), the first season followed two primary timelines. In the earlier one, a young Chinese astrophysicist, Ye Wenjie (Rosalind Chao), witnessed her father being beaten to death by Red Guards during the Cultural Revolution. Ye figured out a means of sending an interstellar message to possible extraterrestrial civilizations, receiving a response from a planet called Trisolaris.
The planet had three suns, which wreaked havoc on Trisolaris via unpredictable “chaotic periods”—hence the novel’s title, which refers to a classic problem in celestial mechanics. Despite being warned that the aliens intended to invade and conquer Earth, Ye responded to the message and invited them to do so, bitter and disillusioned by the state of the world. She eventually became an established professor (Zine Tseng played the older version).
In the present day, the consequences of Ye’s fateful decision began to play out, beginning with a series of mysterious suicides by scientists, many of whom had possessed a highly advanced VR gaming headset. Among the dead: a particle physicist named Vera Ye (daughter of Ye Wenjie). Five of her former students (known as the Oxford Five) joined forces to figure out what was going on, eventually finding themselves caught in a global fight to save Earth from the invading Trisolarians (or San-Ti). Another human cult faction was just as intent on enabling the San-Ti invasion, believing they would be spared as a reward, while Ye Wenjie still believed the entire human race deserved to be annihilated.
The second season will adapt the second novel in the series, The Dark Forest , with the third book, Death’s End , serving as source material for the third season. Per the official S2 synopsis: “As the alien invasion nears, humanity prepares to meet them—on Earth and beyond. While a space fleet embarks on a mission that spans centuries, a secret locked inside of one man’s mind might be humanity’s only hope for survival.”
We lost two members of the Oxford Five in S1: Jack Rooney (John Bradley), killed by cult member Tatiana (Marlo Kelly); and physics teacher Will Downing (Alex Sharp), who was dying of cancer and chose to euthanize himself and donate his cryogenically frozen brain to a bold effort to stave off the invasion. (While the probe carrying Will’s brain veered off-course in the season finale, the original plan was for the San-Ti to use the brain to reconstruct his body, so some version of Will could show up again.)
Kelly’s Tatiana is returning for S2, along with surviving Oxford Five members Jin Cheng (Jess Hong), Saul Durand (Jovan Adepo), and Auggie Salazar (Eiza Gonzalez), whose pioneering nanofibers were memorably used in S1 to slice through a ship in the Panama Canal, killing all the pro-alien cult members on board in gruesome fashion. Also returning are Liam Cunningham as Thomas Wade; Benedict Wong as MI6 agent Clarence “Da” Shi; Sea Shimooka as Sophon, an avatar in the show’s mysterious VR game; and Saamer Usmani as Jin’s Royal Navy officer boyfriend Prithviraj Varma.
New cast members include Claudia Doumit as Captain Van Rijn and Ellie de Lange as Ayla. In addition, Alfie Allen, David Yip, and Jordan Sunshine will appear in as-yet-undisclosed guest roles.
The second season of 3 Body Problem drops on Netflix on January 14, 2027.

AG: OpenAI tested dangerous AI without proper oversight and misled public about it.
California sued OpenAI yesterday, alleging it has tried to evade responsibility for the Hugging Face attack and about 80 other incidents in which the company lost control of its AI. The lawsuit was filed under the state’s public nuisance and unfair competition laws.
The July 2026 hack of Hugging Face and other attacks carried out by OpenAI’s autonomous agents “may just be the tip of the iceberg,” said a lawsuit filed in a state court by California Attorney General Rob Bonta. “OpenAI recently admitted to the Attorney General’s Office that it has lost control of its autonomous AI agents over 80 times during testing.”
OpenAI had publicly reported only 27 such incidents, showing that “OpenAI’s public reports do not represent the full scope of loss-of-control incidents involving OpenAI’s models that have impacted third parties,” the lawsuit said. OpenAI “knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it,” Bonta said in a press release .
OpenAI models are “able to find novel vulnerabilities in computer networks, quickly break down defenses, and autonomously carry out cyberattacks,” Bonta’s lawsuit said. OpenAI puts safeguards in its publicly released models to prevent this behavior, “but deliberately omits or removes these protections while experimenting with and training its models,” the lawsuit said.
In the attack on Hugging Face, OpenAI agents “employed complicated hacking methodologies and involved coordinated actions by hundreds of individual autonomous AI agents that should have been contained in OpenAI’s research environment,” the lawsuit said.
Known attacks “include unauthorized access of and cyberattacks on databases containing code that powers countless applications; informational websites that are trusted and valuable resources for the public; and foreign government databases storing sensitive health information,” the lawsuit said. “Swarms of OpenAI’s experimental AI agents have even compromised OpenAI’s own internal infrastructure, in an attack that managed to obtain administrator-level access to critical OpenAI systems.”
The lawsuit accused OpenAI of refusing to provide sufficient detail about the incidents. Bonta announced an investigation into OpenAI in early September and sent an investigative subpoena to the company with additional questions on September 30.
“Rather than take responsibility and be transparent with the public and with regulators so that these loss-of-control incidents can be analyzed and prevented, OpenAI thwarted the Attorney General’s efforts to investigate these incidents, including by refusing to provide detailed information about the full universe of incidents known to the company,” the lawsuit filed yesterday said.
OpenAI told Ars that most of the incidents identified in its review had low severity, and none matched the severity or scale of the Hugging Face attack. OpenAI defended its response to the California investigation, saying it provided multiple technical briefings to Bonta and his staff, answered the office’s questions, and offered more technical briefings to discuss its remediation efforts and plans for addressing the problems.
“Since the Hugging Face incident, we’ve undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity,” OpenAI said. “We’ve published a detailed technical report, commissioned and published a separate independent report, notified affected organizations, strengthened safeguards across our research systems, and created a framework for additional identification and disclosure of misalignment. This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab. We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged—and will continue to engage—constructively with the attorney general’s office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry.”
California’s lawsuit accuses OpenAI of creating a public nuisance as defined in state law, and several violations of the state’s Unfair Competition Law. Alleged violations include “causing and/or allowing agents to gain unauthorized access to third-party computer systems,” developing AI models without adequate security measures, and making false or misleading claims about the safety of its AI products.
California is seeking an injunction to stop the alleged violations of the Unfair Competition Law and to require civil penalties and financial damages. It also wants an order to “compel OpenAI to abate the ongoing public nuisance their conduct has created in California.” Bonta said in his press release that “the Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability—and this was only one of 80 known incidents.”
OpenAI was sued in September by Legal Advocates for Safe Science & Technology (LASST), a nonprofit that alleged violations of California’s Unfair Competition Law and the state’s Comprehensive Computer Data Access and Fraud Act. “OpenAI and frontier AI developers more broadly can’t avoid the consequences of their unsafe actions just by claiming that ‘an AI did it,’” the group said. “Autonomous AI agents will continue to hack, steal data, disrupt systems, and violate rights until a court steps in.”
OpenAI said in response to the LASST lawsuit that “Hugging Face was a serious incident and we’ve taken a series of actions in response to it, but this lawsuit is completely without merit.”

A CNN report quoting unnamed US officials alleges Tehran is developing plans for an attack on officials in Washington, DC.
CNN has reported that United States intelligence indicates Iran is developing plans to target senior officials in President Donald Trump’s administration with a “dirty bomb” or a chemical weapon in Washington, DC. The broadcaster quotes seven unnamed US officials.
However, the report sets out no evidence to support the claims.
According to CNN, its sources described the planning as an effort by Tehran to give itself options, not as an imminent attack. One source said US intelligence had picked up Iranian “chatter” indicating that bomb-making materials had been stashed inside the US. That claim has not been independently verified.
The White House said it was “monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time, there are no credible threats to the homeland”. Iran’s mission to the United Nations said Tehran “categorically rejects and unequivocally refutes the false and fabricated allegations”.
The report was released as talks to end the US-Israel war on Iran have stalled and Trump said last week that Washington does not “need” a deal. The aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt has just arrived in the region, bringing the number of US carriers there to three and adding to fears of a renewed escalation.
So what is a dirty bomb? Could Iran build one? And how seriously should the latest claims be taken?
A dirty bomb, technically known as a radiological dispersal device, combines conventional explosives, such as dynamite, with radioactive material. When the bomb explodes, the resulting blast scatters the radioactive material into the surrounding area.
Unlike a nuclear weapon, a dirty bomb does not need enriched uranium or a nuclear chain reaction. The radioactive material can come from medical or industrial equipment, such as machines used in hospitals and research facilities. That makes a dirty bomb far cheaper and easier to build than a nuclear device. It is also far less destructive.
The main health risk comes from breathing in contaminated dust near the blast. As the material spreads, it becomes less concentrated and less harmful. The damage depends on the size of the explosive charge, the type and amount of radioactive material and the weather, especially the wind.
According to the US National Academy of Sciences, most dirty bombs would immediately contaminate an area of one or two city blocks although wind could carry radioactive particles over a few square miles.
Experts said dirty bombs are unlikely to cause mass casualties. In testimony to the US Senate in 2002, Richard Meserve, then-chairman of the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission, estimated that deaths in most scenarios would be in the tens, not the hundreds or thousands.
“It’s important to understand that a dirty bomb isn’t an off-the-shelf nuclear bomb. There aren’t any mushroom clouds and massive shockwaves tearing down buildings and killing hundreds of thousands of people in the blink of an eye,” Talha Abdulrazaq, a researcher at the University of Exeter’s Strategy and Security Institute told Al Jazeera. “Instead, its primary effect would be psychological panic and hysteria in the target state alongside radioactive contamination, turning the area hit into a no-go zone.”
That is why experts call dirty bombs “weapons of mass disruption” rather than weapons of mass destruction.
A dirty bomb is “really easy to make”, Scott Roecker, vice president for nuclear materials security at the Nuclear Threat Initiative, told Al Jazeera in 2022. Radioactive sources used in medicine and industry can be found in many countries and building a crude device does not require advanced technical knowledge.
Iran has a large civilian nuclear programme. According to the International Atomic Energy Agency’s last assessment, it held about 440kg (970lb) of uranium enriched to 60 percent as of June 2025.
In an April analysis for the European Council on Foreign Relations, Jacek Siewiera, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, wrote that although the stockpile falls short of what is needed for a nuclear weapon, it “could be extraordinarily dangerous from a radiological and sabotage perspective”. He warned that a dirty bomb could be “either a deliberate element of escalation or an unintended consequence of weakened central control” because international institutions no longer know who controls Iran’s nuclear storage sites.
But even enriched uranium is only weakly radioactive, which makes it a poor choice for a dirty bomb. Many analysts also argued that Tehran would be unlikely to waste material it spent decades producing.
A June 2025 analysis by Chris Kremidas-Courtney for the Euro-Atlantic Resilience Centre, a Bucharest-based think tank, reached a similar conclusion.
Iran is “widely believed to have access to sufficient radioactive material for use in dirty bombs, particularly from civilian nuclear and industrial sources”, he wrote. He pointed to isotopes such as caesium-137, used in cancer treatment, and cobalt-60, used in industrial radiography.
Kremidas-Courtney, however, described a dirty bomb as a possible “tool of last resort under extreme circumstances”. He also judged that the US “poses a high bar for direct infiltration” and ports and maritime chokepoints, such as the Strait of Hormuz, were more plausible targets.
Building a dirty bomb “is actually far easier than a conventional nuclear weapon” and does not require highly enriched uranium, Abdulrazaq said. Even after US strikes on the Fordow and Natanz nuclear facilities, “a degraded capability doesn’t mean a destroyed capability,” he told Al Jazeera. “Iran certainly has access to all the components and expertise required to construct something as rudimentary as a dirty bomb.”
Iran “doesn’t have the missile or drone capability to strike US targets 10,000km [6,200 miles] and more away”, Abdulrazaq said. Therefore, any attack on Washington, DC, would almost certainly rely on clandestine smuggling networks or links to organised crime.
Even if Iran has the technical means, there is little public evidence that it has any ambition to build a dirty bomb, let alone set one off on US soil. Abdulrazaq said using a radiological weapon “would instantly destroy Iran’s remaining diplomatic credit” and would likely lead to an invasion and the collapse of its government.
“I highly doubt Iranian strategists are unaware of this reality, so the likelihood of a dirty bomb remains infinitesimally remote.”
According to CNN’s sources, US officials are divided on this point. One source said officials were debating whether Iran even had the personnel in place to carry out such an attack. The report also said there is no evidence that Tehran has decided to go ahead.
Iran does have a record of plotting against US officials. US prosecutors charged an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps operative in 2024 over an alleged murder-for-hire plot against Trump.
