A major health organisation declares measles endemic in US for first time since 2000, reversing decades of progress.
The United States has officially lost its measles elimination status, reversing a public health achievement maintained for 26 years, as the country grapples with its largest outbreak in more than three decades.
The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) , the Americas branch of the World Health Organization (WHO), declared measles endemic in the US, Bolivia and Mexico on Tuesday after determining that the same strain of the virus had circulated continuously in each country for at least 12 months.
An international panel of experts that advises PAHO on the prevalence of measles and rubella “recommended that the measles elimination status be withdrawn”, said Dr Jarbas Barbosa, director of PAHO, “a recommendation which I have accepted”.
Countries that lost their measles elimination status are required to submit a corrective action plan to PAHO in the coming weeks. PAHO said it will submit its recommendations to the countries in the next few days.
PAHO’s announcement follows a review of epidemiological and laboratory evidence submitted by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
In a joint statement issued on Tuesday, the CDC said it remained committed to stopping measles outbreaks and regaining the country’s elimination status.
“The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does,” CDC Director Erica Schwartz said, adding that the agency would continue working to contain outbreaks.
The CDC said it has provided approximately $100m in additional funding to state and local health departments since August to strengthen vaccination efforts, surveillance and outbreak response.
The US has recorded approximately 7,700 measles infections since the beginning of 2025, according to CDC figures.
It is the highest number of cases the country has seen in more than 30 years. The climbing numbers come as vaccine hesitancy has grown under Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, who has repeatedly cast doubt on the safety of vaccines despite scientific evidence to the contrary.
Before taking office, Kennedy claimed that no vaccine was “safe and effective” and promoted the discredited theory that vaccines cause autism.
To protect against illness, children are commonly given the measles vaccine in a combined shot with mumps and rubella vaccines, known by the acronym MMR.
But the vaccination rate among preschoolers in the US has fallen to about 92 percent, below the level experts say is needed to prevent major outbreaks.
As health secretary under US President Donald Trump, Kennedy has questioned the MMR vaccine’s ability to protect children.
He has suggested that the MMR vaccine’s effectiveness wanes by about 4.5 percent a year and said it contains “aborted fetus debris”, a claim experts have rejected as false .
The CDC has confirmed six measles-related deaths this year, but state health officials in Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and New York have reported 10 deaths combined, a discrepancy that has fuelled tensions between federal and state health authorities over how measles deaths are classified and counted.
Measles is considered highly infectious, and the WHO estimates the virus caused 95,000 deaths worldwide in 2024, mostly among children.
Matt Ferrari, a biology professor and director of Pennsylvania State University’s Center for Infectious Disease Dynamics, believes the loss of the US’s measles elimination status can serve as a wake-up call for public health officials.
“This should be a humbling statement for the United States,” Ferrari told Al Jazeera.
For much of his career, Ferrari has studied strategies to control measles in countries around the world. The US was previously seen as a model.
“It was a motivating achievement that we use to drive support for measles elimination programmes all around the world,” said Ferrari. “Now we need to be looking for expertise elsewhere because we haven’t been pulling our weight.”
Edwin Asturias, a professor of paediatrics, infectious disease and epidemiology at the University of Colorado, described the loss of status as a “stain” on the country’s public health programme.
“Measles cases are a signal that your immunisation programme and other systems within your public health services are having problems,” he told Al Jazeera.
Asturias said the US had the resources and experience to prevent the resurgence of the virus, pointing to its success in eliminating local measles transmission for more than a quarter of a century.
About 40 percent of current US measles cases are among adults older than 20, he said, highlighting the need to expand vaccination efforts.
Reaching these populations will require making vaccines available in workplaces, places of worship and other community settings, rather than relying solely on paediatricians and family doctors, Asturias explained.
The loss of elimination status also has implications beyond US borders , as measles can spread through international travel and migration.
“The United States is not, any more, a place where you’re safe from measles,” Asturias told Al Jazeera. “If you’re a common person walking around with your children, you need to know now that measles has come to the country to stay unless something else is done.”
The risk is particularly concerning for unvaccinated people and those who cannot receive the vaccine, including those with weakened immune systems or people undergoing cancer treatment.
Public health experts say the announcement should serve as a catalyst for a more extensive vaccination response.
While they do not expect PAHO’s announcement to prompt a significant change in federal policy, some hope it will spur action among state and local health departments.
Ferrari argued that the US should look to countries with experience containing measles outbreaks, including India, where community health workers visit households to identify children who may have missed vaccinations or whose families may be reluctant to vaccinate.
He also suggested that states may need to reconsider vaccination strategies, including whether to offer an earlier first or second dose to protect young children in areas where measles is circulating.
In the US, children are routinely given two doses of the MMR vaccine. The first dose is typically administered to children at 12 to 15 months of age and the second at four to six years, before they start school. Two doses are about 97 percent effective at preventing measles.
In countries where measles transmission is more widespread, the second MMR dose is often given between the ages of 18 and 24 months.
In June, Pennsylvania began recommending an additional early dose, called a “dose zero”, for infants aged six months and older in areas with sustained measles transmission. Ferrari said this was a perfect example of how states could adapt their approaches locally.
But the prospect of a broader shift in the federal response remains unlikely.
CDC Director Schwartz said last week the agency would continue “doing the same exact thing” in terms of its measles response if the US lost its elimination status.
For Asturias, the federal response so far raises concerns about whether the country has the public health leadership needed to reverse the outbreak.
“This is hard to see happen,” he said. “But at the same time, it is predictable when you don’t have experts running a public healthcare system.”

BBC's Madeline Halpert explains why the US lost its measles elimination status and what it could mean.
After more than two decades, the US has lost its measles-free status, following two years of record case numbers and deaths.
The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a specialised service of the United Nations, determined the US has had uninterrupted transmission of the same strain of measles for more than 12 months.
Dr Jarbas Barbosa, director of PAHO, announced that Mexico and Bolivia have also lost their measles elimination status, attributing the resurgence in the region to persistent "gaps in vaccination".
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said it was committed to "regaining measles elimination status" by expanding access to vaccines.
The US has seen 5,400 cases of measles this year alone, with 10 measles-related deaths, the most the country has seen since the 1990s.
The measles virus - with its signature blotchy red rash - used to infect millions of children a year before a vaccine was invented. The extremely contagious virus can be fatal, and some patients can experience long-term complications including encephalitis and immune amnesia, which resets the immune system, leaving it with only limited ability to respond to new infections.
The US recommends two measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) shots for children between ages one and six, which is 97% effective in protecting against the illness.
PAHO, a group within the World Health Organization, revoked the US's measles-elimination after determining that the virus had circulated nonstop for more than a year.
"These figures are a serious warning for our region," PAHO's director Barbosa said at a news conference on Tuesday. "Measles is resurging globally amid persistent gaps in vaccination."
He added that Canada, which lost its status of having eliminated measles last year after seeing several large outbreaks, has made strides this year to interrupt transmission.
Daniel Salas, the executive manager of immunisations at PAHO, said that the US and others who lost elimination status would be required to submit corrective action plans outlining how they would attempt to improve vaccination rates.
US Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr Kennedy has attempted to make a series of sweeping changes to US vaccine recommendations and policies. The vaccine sceptic has also frequently cast doubt on the safety of MMR shot, as vaccination rates have declined across the US in recent years.
Kennedy has argued that the rise in measles cases started before he took the helm at HHS and that neighbouring countries have also seen more infections.
Responding to Tuesday's announcement, the CDC said the agency and its partners were "committed to stopping measles outbreaks, protecting Americans, and regaining measles elimination status".
"Together, we will encourage MMR vaccination, expand access to vaccines, and help communities close gaps in protection," the agency said.
CDC Director Erica Schwartz said the measles elimination designation was not what protected Americans.
"Vaccination does," she said. "We know where transmission is occurring and we've invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach those communities."
The UK, Spain and Austria were among European nations that lost their measles-free status earlier this year, along with countries including Russia, Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan.
Nuwan Gunawardhana, an assistant professor of medicine with Columbia University Irving Medical Center, said the US losing its elimination status was "a huge leap backwards".
The US was the first country to eliminate measles in the Americas thanks to vaccination campaigns, noted William Moss, a paediatric infectious disease specialist at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.
Dr Gunawardhana said it took massive efforts from public health officials and clinicians to build trust with patients to increase uptake of the MMR vaccine, leading to decades in the US with few infections and deaths.
But that trust has been steadily eroding since the Covid-19 pandemic, when Dr Gunawardhana said patients were confronted with misinformation about the safety of vaccines and lost even more trust in public health systems.
The vaccination rate for MMR across the US has fallen to 92.4%, below the 95% level that provides herd immunity, which limits the spread of measles and protects those who cannot get vaccinated, including newborns.
The vaccination rate for MMR across the US has fallen to 92.4%, below the 95% level that provides herd immunity - which limits the spread of measles
An outbreak in Pennsylvania has infected over 1,400 people - likely a large underestimate - and killed seven people, according to state officials.
Kennedy, the health secretary, has sparred with Pennsylvania officials over how it is counting the measles deaths, with CDC declining for now to record some of the deaths in its database.
Last year, the health secretary fired all the members of a top vaccine advisory panel and replaced them with his own appointees, some of whom were vaccine critics.
The panel recommended a number of vaccine changes - including no longer requiring the Hepatitis B vaccine for all newborns - but those recommendations were blocked by a federal judge.
President Donald Trump this year also cast doubt on the safety of the MMR vaccine, issuing an executive order for the shot to be split into three separate immunisations for measles, mumps and rubella, a move public health experts say is costly and could sow confusion about an already safe vaccine.
Doctors and public health officials say the misinformation from Kennedy and Trump has played a major role in falling vaccination rates.
"It's confusing patients. It's confusing families," Dr Gunawardhana said. "We need a clear message from the top."
The federal government's vaccine manoeuvres have left public health officials and states to fill in the gaps, offering their own separate recommendations upholding decades-long practices.

FILE - A freight train runs on rails of a railway link of the Crimean Bridge connecting Russian mainland and Crimean peninsula over the Kerch Strait not far from Kerch, Crimea, on Monday, July 17, 2023. AP Photo//AP hide caption
A Ukrainian drone and missile attack prepared over several weeks struck a vital Russian rail and road bridge to the occupied Crimean Peninsula, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Tuesday, in a stunning blow after nearly five years of war.
Zelenskyy portrayed the "unprecedented" operation on the Kerch Bridge as a masterstroke, as Ukrainian forces gradually wore down Russian air defenses before bombarding the prized target with missiles and drones overnight.
He didn't detail the damage but unconfirmed media reports said that a span of the bridge collapsed in the attack, in what would be an embarrassing setback for Moscow.
The Russian-installed governor of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, said that traffic across the bridge has been halted and urged people "to refrain from trips in the direction of the bridge." He didn't mention any damage.
The Kerch Bridge is a crucial link in moving military and civilian supplies from Russia to Crimea and to support troops on the front line. The construction of the bridge, a potent symbol of Russia's illegal annexation of the peninsula in 2014, was inflammatory for Ukrainians.
Moscow's forces, meanwhile, fired ballistic missiles and drones at Kyiv, hitting two of the Ukrainian capital's main bridges and killing at least two people.
A recent escalation in aerial attacks came as Russia and Ukraine await a date for the next round of U.S.-mediated talks aimed at ending the war that began with Moscow's full-scale invasion of its neighbor on Feb. 24, 2022.
U.S. President Donald Trump says he plans to talk about the war in Ukraine during his highly anticipated meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in China this week.
The Kerch Bridge attack was the culmination of weeks of preparatory strikes over seven stages of the operation, Zelenskyy said on social media.
Ukrainian forces knocked out defense systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment and other designated targets before launching Monday night's final attack, he said.
Domestically developed long-range drones struck the bridge's road section during the night while Ukraine's Neptune missiles and other drones aimed at the rail section, he said. Flamingo precision-guided missiles delivered the final blow, he said.
Russia's Investigative Committee said that the bridge was attacked by drones on both days and sustained damage. It didn't elaborate on the extent of the damage.
Zelenskyy noted that Russia has battered Ukrainian infrastructure, especially the power grid, every day.
"We have repeatedly offered Russia steps toward de-escalation — and every proposal has been met with loud rejection," he said.
Russian air defenses downed 1,441 drones during a second straight night of major Ukrainian attacks, Russia's Defense Ministry said Tuesday.
On Monday, Russia said that it downed 1,336 Ukrainian drones in the highest number of interceptions it had reported so far during the war.
Elsewhere, authorities in Bashkortostan, a Russian region in the south of Russia's Ural Mountains, said that defenses repelled a "massive" drone attack on industrial zones of the cities of Ufa and Salavat. All plants there worked as usual, and no critical damage has been inflicted on them, officials said.
Independent news outlet Astra, however, reported a huge fire at the Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat oil refining and petrochemical complex, located nearly 1,300 kilometers (800 miles) east of the Ukrainian border. The complex has been attacked a number of times before.
In Moscow, Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said that around 800 drones flew toward the Moscow region overnight. Most were downed far away, and 321 were shot down as they approached the Russian capital.
Experts are inspecting Kyiv's North and South bridges, damaged in a Russian ballistic missile attack, to assess the extent of the destruction, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Tuesday morning.
Russian attacks damaged other infrastructure and started fires in four districts of the Ukrainian capital, officials said, as Moscow continues its campaign to make life difficult for Ukrainian civilians.
The Russian Defense Ministry said Tuesday that its forces overnight carried out a major strike using land- and air-based precision weapons and drones on Ukraine's military industrial facilities, energy, transport and port infrastructure, as well as vessels used for Ukraine's armed forces.
Russian forces launched a combined attack on industrial facilities in three districts of the southern Ukraine region of Zaporizhzhia, killing two people and wounding 18 others and leaving a large number of consumers in the region without power, said Mykhailo Semikin, head of the Zaporizhzhia Regional Military Administration.
Meanwhile, the negotiating teams of Ukraine, the United States, and European partners held a working video call on Monday, during which they discussed the results of recent talks in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, and the agenda for the next stage of negotiations, said Rustem Umerov, head of Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service.
"We aligned our positions and our next joint steps," Umerov said on Telegram following the conversation.
On the European side, representatives of France, Germany, the United Kingdom, Italy, Poland, NATO and the European Commission joined the conversation.
The United States was represented by envoys Steve Witkoff, Jared Kushner, and Alexus Grynkewich, the commander of U.S. forces in Europe, Umerov said.

A Palestinian woman in her 70s has been shot dead, and several other people wounded, in a village in the occupied West Bank where Israeli settlers recently moved in, the Palestinian health ministry says.
There are conflicting accounts of what happened. Local Palestinians said there was an attack by settlers in part of al-Duyuk al-Tahta, near Jericho, which is meant to be under the full control of the Palestinian Authority.
According to the Israeli army, there was a Palestinian car-ramming attack on an Israeli vehicle. It said rocks were then thrown at the Israelis, who opened fire in response. It did not mention the fatal shooting of a woman.
There have been high tensions in the area since a group of settlers recently set up a new outpost.
They moved into eight houses in the village on 4 November after buying them, they have said, in a secretive operation. The properties are in an area where Israel retains full security control.
Medics say Palestinians and Israelis were wounded in the incident on Monday evening
Local Palestinians said that the events in al-Duyuk al-Tahta on Monday night began with harassment by Israeli settlers. Children threw stones, they said, and the settlers opened fire, killing Fadda al-Fahidat, who was 72, outside her home.
According to Palestinian accounts, her son rushed to the scene in his car after hearing the news and collided with an empty Israeli settler car parked outside his family home, injuring settlers who were standing nearby. The settlers then fired more shots, they said.
The statement from the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said that "terrorists accelerated their vehicle toward an Israeli vehicle and rammed it", and then "exited their vehicle with weapons and attacked and harmed the occupants of the Israeli vehicle".
Afterwards, it said, "rocks were hurled at the Israelis, who responded by firing in order to remove the threat."
The IDF said that Israeli security forces were sent to the scene and were pursuing suspects.
Doctors at a hospital in Jericho said that al-Fahidat was shot in the head. Several other Palestinians and Israelis were injured, reports said.
The Israeli human rights group B'Tselem says there has been a prolonged campaign of settler attacks, intimidation and land seizures in al-Duyuk al-Tahta, with Israeli troops now stationed nearby to secure the new settlement.
Residents and activists say armed settlers walk and drive quad bikes around the neighbourhood as they threaten Palestinian residents.
A group of settlers set up a new outpost in al-Duyuk al-Tahta earlier this month (file photo)
In a separate incident on Monday evening, eight Palestinians were injured when they were hit by a vehicle driven by an Israeli settler on a main road in Tuqu, south of Bethlehem, according to Palestinian officials and the Palestinian Red Crescent.
The IDF said the incident was a traffic accident. But the Palestinian foreign ministry called it a "terrorist attack", saying the driver hit a group of Palestinians who had gathered near the scene of an earlier traffic accident.

The E1 area east of Jerusalem is a strategically important part of the occupied West Bank
The UK has sanctioned companies it said are involved in building settlements in the occupied West Bank, in the first package of measures since the government announced a tougher approach to Israeli actions in the territory.
The government said the sanctions against eight construction and property development firms would disrupt their flows of finance and ability to support building in the West Bank.
The construction of settlements, which are illegal under international law, has risen sharply in recent years. Settler attacks on Palestinians and their property have also surged.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar called the sanctions a "hostile act targeting private, law-abiding companies".
Criticising the move on X, he wrote that Israel - as it has done in the past - will respond with "countermeasures", and that "decisions will be announced in due course".
"Israel will not bow to external pressure or change its policies as a result," Saar said, adding that they will "consider new ways to strengthen Jewish communities" in the West Bank, and "protect those involved in developing and building".
Israel previously condemned UK sanctions related to West Bank settlements, accusing the Labour government of "systematically acting against the State of Israel".
The Palestinian foreign ministry welcomed the sanctions and called on other countries to follow suit.
It comes two days before the deadline for bids for construction tenders in the highly sensitive E1 area east of Jerusalem.
The plans, which have been condemned internationally, would in effect divide the West Bank in two and cut it off from East Jerusalem.
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has said the E1 development would render a two-state solution "unviable" by "cutting through the heart of Palestine".
The sanctions also target Tzav 9, an Israeli activist movement which the UK government says has organised and carried out blockades to prevent aid entering Gaza.
Responding to the announcement, the group said: "Tzav 9 is a movement of abiding citizens from all the political spectrum, and we've always protested peacefully."
It comes after the UK expanded its human rights sanctions regime last month, enabling the government to sanction individuals and companies involved in violations of international humanitarian law anywhere in the world.
The government is also developing separate legislation to ban the import of goods from Israeli settlements and the provision of advertising services for settlement properties in the UK.
Miliband said: "Protecting the two-state solution is the North Star of this government's approach.
"That is why my message on E1 is clear: do not bid, do not build, and do not profit from the destruction of the two-state solution.
"We are committed to working productively with a new Israeli government and the Palestinian Authority to advance lasting peace and security for Israelis and Palestinians alike."
In September, the UK government announced that it would ban the import of goods from Israeli settlements, as well as acting against companies and individuals providing services for settlement expansion.
At the time, Miliband said the move marked the beginning of a "new approach" to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, which "not only calls out injustice and suffering, but acts".
That announcement prompted a furious reaction from Israel , which said it would shut the British consulate in East Jerusalem in retaliation.
Last month, most diplomats left the consulate - which handled UK relations with Palestinians in Jerusalem as well as in the West Bank and Gaza - but the UK insisted that the building would not be closing and would operate as a "UK mission".
Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jews since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem during the 1967 Middle East war. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them.
There has been a surge in attacks by settlers on Palestinians and their property in the West Bank since the start of the Gaza war, which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023.

Infectious disease is now continually spreading after being eliminated for 26 years, with more than 5,400 US cases
The US lost its measles elimination status, global health authorities announced, an official recognition that the infectious disease is endemic in the US after being eliminated for 26 years.
The announcement comes as the US endures the worst measles outbreak since 1991, with more than 5,400 cases and eight deaths in 2026.
“Measles is resurging globally amid the persistent gaps in vaccination coverage, and this global trend is also affecting the Americas,” said Dr Jarbas Barbosa da Silva Jr, the director of the Pan American Health Organization, a regional branch of the World Health Organization . “The endemic measles transmission has now been re-established in Bolivia, Mexico and United States.” Silva made the final decision on US elimination status.
Measles is one of the most contagious viruses known to medicine and requires 95% of the community to be vaccinated to prevent outbreaks. The measles vaccine is safe and highly effective. However, pockets of low vaccination have grown in the US following pandemic-era disruptions and widespread misinformation.
The nation’s largest doctors group, the American Medical Association, described loss of measles elimination status as a “deeply troubling and entirely preventable setback for our nation”.
The loss of measles-free status comes after Donald Trump and his health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr , spent nearly two years sowing confusion about the safety of vaccines. In just one recent example, Trump called for the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) combination vaccine to be split into separate shots, arguing without evidence that “together, there could be a possibility they’re quite lethal”.
“As a pediatrician, I saw firsthand how decisions made in Washington hurt our children and families,” said Dr Annie Andrews, a Democratic senator-elect. “Nothing makes that clearer than the loss of our measles elimination status.” The loss of elimination status has already heightened criticism of Kennedy. High-profile epidemiologists called Kennedy’s work at the health department “malpractice” and equivalent to a “crime scene”.
Barbosa called the role of misinformation in measles transmission “dynamic” and urged health departments to develop bespoke campaigns tailored to under-vaccinated communities.
Experts caution against piling blame for measles outbreaks solely on the Trump administration . The MMR vaccine has been the target of misinformation for more than two decades, including work by Kennedy before his White House role.
“There is a profound problem with measles in all three North American countries,” said Noel Brewer, a behavioral scientist at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill who studies vaccination behaviors, and specifically measles. He chairs a committee that considers evidence on US measles elimination status, and contributed to the scientific work that underpinned Pan American Health Organization (Paho)’s decision.“The US has had large outbreaks and exported those to Canada and Mexico, and those cases have come back again to the US,” said Brewer.
Canada lost its measles-free status in 2025, but Barbosa said the country now represented the “good news” in the region. The nation stopped measles transmission for 60 days. This is the first step on the way to regaining measles elimination status. The UK and several European nations have also recently lost elimination status.
“What we’re experiencing is not a United States specific thing,” said David Margolius of the Big Cities Health Coalition. Instead, there is a, “global surge in cases, global decline in vaccination rate”.
Public health leaders with the Big Cities Health Coalition (BHC), which leads health departments that serve 47 million Americans, described the announcement as a “profoundly sad moment for our country”.
“Recent declines in measles vaccination rates have opened the door to outbreaks across the country, resulting in preventable illness, hospitalizations, and tragic loss of life,” BHC members said in a statement . “These outcomes are especially heartbreaking because measles is a disease that we know how to prevent. Yet too many voices spreading fear and false information are exacerbating the problem.”
Expert epidemiologists recommended US measles status change during a closed-door meeting in Washington DC. A range of evidence would have been presented, including interviews with positive patients collected by local US health authorities and whole genome sequencing that can provide a fingerprint of the virus’s origin.
Although measles elimination status is an official designation, it carries real consequences for Americans. Where measles cases were once typically imported by international travelers, endemic measles transmission means Americans face new risks of infection, and are being asked to dig up decades-old vaccination certificates and possibly quarantine for 21 days.
“Now is the time to go and find that evidence, because now this is a real day-to-day life thing that could happen to you,” Margolius said earlier in November.
Re-establishing elimination status will require “a national plan to eliminate measles again”, said Brewer, “an integrated plan that’s publicly communicated with specific tasks assigned to named parties”. He added that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the president should speak out “forcefully” in favor of vaccination , and Congress should allocate more funding.

Hundreds hail Student List lawmakers as the new parliament meets for the first time.
Following the October 25 vote that upended Serbia’s political landscape, the new parliament is meeting for the first time in Belgrade.
The vote redrew Serbia’s parliamentary map as a grassroots, student-led movement won the largest single share, removing President Aleksandar Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS).
The Student List group was backed by 2.3 million citizens, altering the previous parliamentary arithmetic and balance of power. It holds a majority with 140 parliamentary seats in the 250-member parliament, compared with the Serbian Progressive Party’s 104.
Tuesday’s session is chaired by the oldest member of parliament until a new speaker is elected, assisted by the four youngest MPs from the largest electoral lists. Hundreds of supporters cheered the new lawmakers as they entered the National Assembly. The new speaker could be announced later on Tuesday.
The formal agenda follows a clear legal framework: verifying parliamentary mandates based on a report by the Republic Electoral Commission (RIK), taking the solemn oath of office, electing the speaker and deputy speakers, appointing the secretary-general, and forming parliamentary committees and permanent delegations to international bodies.
But beyond legal formalities, the political atmosphere is complex and large sections of the public have high expectations.
Political analyst Djordje Vukadinovic told Al Jazeera, “Everyone is eagerly awaiting it. I would avoid making any predictions, because with the current opposition structure, you never know what might happen or what stance they will take.”
He added, “What I do know is that this is only the beginning of establishing a new government, and I believe not everything will be wrapped up today.”
Ahead of the session, a group of students wrote to the new lawmakers, reminding them of their “serious” responsibilities.
“All of you are becoming members of parliament in the highest legislative body of the Republic of Serbia for the first time. And only that. Nothing more. The fact that the highest state offices have for decades been presented as ‘comfortable armchairs’ is a systemic flaw. The people elected you. We are the people. You are the people. Act accordingly,” warned the Student Plenum of the Higher School of Civil Engineering and Geodesy in Belgrade in an open letter.
Aleksandar Cupic, an incoming Student List MP and an assistant professor in engineering, said new lawmakers must demonstrate institutional maturity.
“We do not plan to speak about our candidate for five or 10 hours, because that is neither in the spirit of the values we will represent nor is it rational. We owe it to the citizens to proceed with electing the speaker of parliament,” Cupic told reporters ahead of the session.
He said political groups had been consulting one another in a more moderate atmosphere than reports have suggested.
A woman threw yoghurt over Lidija Vukicevic, a well known actress who supports the SNS, outside parliament and the crowd booed Vucic as he walked in.
The Serbian actress and former MP Lidija Vukicevic, who is backing the ruling SNS party, had yoghurt poured over her as she arrived at Serbia’s National Assembly for its first session following elections won by a student-led opposition movement.
The swearing-in session marks the start of a critical political countdown – a 90-day constitutional deadline to elect a new government.
Should that expire without parliament voting in a new cabinet, Serbia’s constitution mandates the dissolution of the National Assembly and the calling of snap parliamentary elections.
The developments are being watched across the region, as well as in European and global political circles.
Observers say the new political leaders will have to govern the state and rebuild sustainable cooperation with neighbouring countries and the European Union – ties that have been strained in recent years.
Echoing that point, Student List representative Aleksandar Baucal told the international EU Enlargement Forum in Brussels that a peaceful transfer of power is only the start of a complex array of work.
“Changing power through non-violent and democratic means is only the first step,” Baucal said in Brussels. “Serbia now faces the task of rebuilding institutions that will prevent the personalisation of power and serve all citizens, regardless of who they voted for. I am convinced that from now on, the news coming out of Serbia will be largely positive.”
In a similar vein, the European Democratic Party (EDP) weighed in on the eve of the parliamentary session.
“Serbia must now heal the wounds of recent years through truth, justice and accountability … we sincerely hope a new chapter of freedom, democracy and reconciliation will begin,” the EDP said, adding that the session will test whether Serbia is ready for institutional reform.

A woman holds an Iranian flag as part of a pro-government campaign beneath a billboard depicting a launched missile, a man with a rifle, people and current and the late Revolutionary Guard missile force commanders with clenched fists, with a sign which reads in Farsi: "The sky is a place for our pride and loyalty," in downtown Tehran, Iran, Monday. Vahid Salemi/AP hide caption
CAIRO — Iran fired drones on Tuesday at a U.S. radar facility in Bahrain, its third attack in recent days on American military targets in the tiny island kingdom in the Persian Gulf after a roughly two-month lull in fighting.
After issuing an alert about the incoming fire, Bahrain said that its air defense systems had successfully intercepted the "treacherous Iranian aerial attacks."
The U.S. military said there was no damage to U.S. equipment or injury to American personnel.
The attacks have brought condemnations from the region, while analysts say that Tehran's growing economic pressures and stalled peace negotiations are raising the risk of renewed escalation.
Iran has been suffering under a naval blockade that the U.S. has enforced on it for months in and around the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial waterway for the world's energy supplies where Iran and its proxies have disrupted shipping since the war began Feb. 28.
U.S. President Donald Trump has been circumspect on his next steps for the Iran war, now in its eighth month despite an initial promise it would last only a matter of weeks. He has said new strikes are highly unlikely, but he has also sent a third aircraft carrier and thousands more troops to the Middle East — and told Vice President JD Vance that talks aren't needed at this time.
Oil tankers moving oil through the strait under U.S. military protection have helped return oil shipments from the Gulf to roughly prewar levels. The blockade, meanwhile, is damaging Iran's economy by curbing the flow of Iranian crude to the global market.
This is a locator map for the Gulf Cooperation Council member states: Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar, Oman, Kuwait and United Arab Emirates. AP hide caption
Iran's attacks could signal a shift in its strategy after months during which it waited for an attack and then retaliated to target the operational capability of bases, Tehran-based security analyst Mostafa Najafi told The Associated Press.
Bahrain hosts the U.S. Navy's 5th Fleet, which has already sustained damage in previous attacks by Iran since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28.
Iranian leaders will now be weighing whether "breaking the blockade through escalation is less costly than accepting its continuation," Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group think tank, wrote in an analysis posted to X.
"In other words, the risk of renewed war no longer depends solely on whether Trump decides to attack Iran again," he said. "It also depends on whether Tehran concludes that the costs of continued restraint have become greater than the risks of escalation."
With the arrival of the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group in the region, the combined U.S. naval assets in the Persian Gulf, Arabian Sea, Red Sea, and Mediterranean now exceed the force deployed when the U.S. and Israel launched the war.
The presence provides greater offensive firepower and missile interception capacity, according to a new analysis by Israel's Institute for National Security Studies.
The Roosevelt joins the USS George H.W. Bush and the USS George Washington aircraft carriers, as well as smaller U.S. Navy ships, which are in the region to maintain the blockade of Iranian shipping. U.S. Central Command wouldn't comment on whether it plans to keep all three carrier strike groups in the region.
Iran's attack on Bahrain on Tuesday came after it targeted a U.S. early warning radar facility in the country on Friday, and on Sunday fired at a radar system at an American helicopter base there. Despite claims of success, there appeared to be little or no damage done.
The attacks followed U.S. strikes on Iranian communications towers and ongoing drone surveillance operations, and Iran said it was retaliating.
"Continued aggression against the country's airspace, as well as the use of regional military bases and facilities for hostile acts against Iran, will not go unanswered," Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps said in a statement.
Egypt, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates each condemned Iran's attack on Bahrain, calling it a violation of Bahrain's sovereignty and a threat to its security and stability.
Negotiations to end the war have stagnated, despite intensified mediation efforts from Qatar.
In a statement, Qatar said Iran's "continued attacks" on Bahrain "undermine diplomatic efforts" and Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed Al Ansari, speaking at a news briefing in Doha, warned that any escalation in fighting posed an "extremely grave danger" to the prospects of reaching an agreement.
The attacks are a sign that Tehran is growing impatient as its economic woes mount, said Sascha Bruchmann, a Bahrain-based defense analyst with the International Institute for Strategic Studies.
"Shooting at ships causes fear, but is not effective enough to change the strategic equation," Bruchmann told the AP. "Tehran knows it needs to do something, but I wouldn't overestimate what we saw against Bahrain this week. This is not it — yet."
Iranian officials have termed the current situation "no war, no peace" and vowed to end it.
Tehran has said that it's open to a negotiated deal, but also signaled a readiness to escalate the conflict in the face of tightening sanctions and the blockade that are throttling Iran's economy.
Mahdi Mohammadi, an adviser to Iran's influential parliamentary chief, posted on social media on Monday that leaders view U.S. economic pressure as an effort to create a domestic "security crisis."
Iran has also continued to attack ships seeking to transit the Strait of Hormuz, which leads from the Persian Gulf toward the open seas.
On Tuesday, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said that a tanker was reportedly attacked twice north of Oman, and that the second strike caused a fire on board. It also received a report that a cargo vessel off the coast of Yemen repelled an attempt by armed men in a skiff to board it.
Iran's Fars news agency reported that two ships were struck by mines in the strait, causing them to catch fire. It wasn't immediately clear whether one was the incident reported by the British military's UKMTO.
In Yemen, Iran-backed Houthi rebels now have solidified their control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, another critical shipping route, which connects the Gulf of Aden to the Red Sea, after a group allied with the Saudi-backed Yemeni government retreated over the weekend in a setback to the anti-Houthi coalition.

President Trump is off for a series of meetings in Asia that will cover trade, security and a rare trilateral meeting with China and Russia.
STEVE INSKEEP, HOST: President Trump's plane has landed in Manila to meet with allies at the ASEAN summit. MICHEL MARTIN, HOST: It's a short visit. Tomorrow he's headed to Shenzhen, China, for another summit. He will meet with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin. It's the first time those three have had a joint summit. INSKEEP: Lots of meetings. NPR White House correspondent Deepa Shivaram is awaiting the president's arrival in Shenzhen, which is one of China's big tech cities. Hi there, Deepa. DEEPA SHIVARAM, BYLINE: Hello. INSKEEP: OK. The president's been spending a fair amount of time with China's leader. I guess they'll spend some more together. SHIVARAM: Yeah, that's right. This is going to be the third time that Trump and Xi meet. Trump went to China earlier this year and then later on hosted Xi at the White House. This meeting, though, will be a little different because it's on the sidelines of the APEC summit that Xi is hosting here in Shenzhen. If you recall, about a year ago, Steve, Trump and Xi met on the sidelines of this same summit in Busan, South Korea, but at that time, tensions between the U.S. and China were really high because of the escalating trade war. And what came out of that meeting last year was, one, an agreement to keep meeting and, two, a sort of economic truce called the Busan Agreement. That involved things like the U.S. lowering tariffs and China loosening controls on rare earths. And it's generally cooled down the temperature between the U.S. and China, but both sides still have some issues. One expert described the agreement to me as not perfect but functional. So what's expected to come from the meeting this week between Xi and Trump is working to extend that agreement, which is set to expire in January. INSKEEP: OK. Just maintaining the status quo. SHIVARAM: Yes. INSKEEP: But we mentioned the president is stopping in the Philippines on the way to China. How does that stopover fit in with the broader U.S. focus on China? SHIVARAM: Yeah, it's a good question. Trump there is expected to meet with the leaders of the Quad. So in addition to the U.S., that includes India, Australia and Japan. These are major democratic nations, and this group was formed to balance power in the Pacific region against China. So timing-wise, it's pretty significant that Trump is able to meet with them before he meets with Xi in China. That will be one part of it. The other part is another trade agreement. The White House says Trump will sign a trade deal with Thailand while he's in the Philippines. INSKEEP: I guess, in a way, it comes across as a show of respect. You stop with the allies before you go and talk with the adversaries. SHIVARAM: In a way, yeah. INSKEEP: So he meets with China's leader then, eventually, where you are in Shenzhen. He's going to meet the regional allies on the way. Why also meet in a single room with both President Xi and President Vladimir Putin of Russia? SHIVARAM: Right. So this is going to be a pretty historic meeting. These three leaders have never met together. Trump has been saying for a while now that he wants to discuss denuclearization with Xi and Putin. But I will say it's not really a topic that China is keen to get into. Trump has also said he wants to discuss with them, you know, about the war in Iran. And on Friday, the White House told reporters that the issue of Ukraine was not going to be on the agenda in this trilateral meeting. That has shifted possibly slightly because when Trump was leaving the White House on Monday, he told reporters that they'll talk about his, quote, "favorite subject" of Ukraine. This is going to be interesting to watch, Steve, because how Ukraine gets discussed in this meeting and what might come out of it has Europe really concerned, has Ukraine very concerned because their president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, will not be at APEC, and recently, Trump has been more lenient towards Putin and Russia. INSKEEP: Wow. One more thing to ask about. Could the president, since he's meeting with so many other people, also have a meeting with Kim Jong Un of North Korea? SHIVARAM: He says that that might happen. It's probably not going to happen. We're still watching to see how things develop. The White House said that they're not planning for this to happen. Logistically, it would be very complicated. But Trump, you know, kind of did this last year, too, saying that he might meet with him in Korea, and that did not end up happening. INSKEEP: NPR's Deepa Shivaram. Thanks so much. SHIVARAM: Thank you.

President Donald Trump inspects an honor guard after stepping off Air Force One, Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026, at Ninoy Aquino International Airport in Manila, Philippines. Mark Schiefelbein/AP hide caption
MANILA, Philippines — President Donald Trump arrived in the Philippines on Tuesday, where he was scheduled to meet regional partners, talk trade, and seek a break from a series of setbacks at home, ranging from a major disruption to the U.S. aviation industry to a scandal that has shaken the global AI industry.
Manila, the Philippine capital, is Trump's first stop on a three-day trip that will later take him to China for historic three-way nuclear talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, and, according to Trump, potentially for a meeting with North Korea's leader Kim Jong Un.
The visit marks Trump's first travel abroad since his party suffered deep losses in midterm elections. The White House and stock market alike have been rattled by the departure of Jensen Huang from Nvidia last week after admitting to an affair with an alleged Chinese government agent. Beijing has said it was not involved.
As he descended the stairs from Air Force One, Trump pumped his fist. A child handed him small American and Philippine flags, which Trump waved and then swooped in big circular motions as he smiled. The U.S. president was greeted by a marching band playing "YMCA" while he walked to a waiting helicopter.
Trump's first hours in the Philippines will include all the reassuring optics from Washington's oldest treaty ally in Asia, including a cocktail reception and dinner with other world leaders, an intermission from some of the thorniest issues at home. He's being feted Tuesday night at a gala as the "guest of honor" at the annual summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.
The ASEAN leaders have been working on a non-aggression pact with China in the contested waters of the South China Sea, a key global trade route. Confrontations have escalated in recent years, particularly between Chinese and Philippine coast guard and naval forces in disputed shoals.
First on Trump's agenda Tuesday is a meeting with the leaders of the Quad nations, comprising the U.S., Australia, India, and Japan that have aimed to counter China's influence in the Asia Pacific. It will be their first meeting since Trump returned to the White House last year.
Trump is then scheduled to sign a trade deal with Thailand, the type of agreement he has relished striking since launching a trade war last year buttressed by steep tariff threats.
The U.S. had announced a trade framework last October in which Thailand would remove tariffs on most American goods, as well as barriers for importing U.S. autos, food products and pharmaceutical drugs, according to the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative. At the time, the Trump administration said Thailand would also spend more than $18 billion on U.S. aircraft and buy U.S. farm goods and liquefied natural gas.
The U.S. Supreme Court overturned in February the 19% tariff that Trump placed on goods from Thailand. The administration sought replacement tariffs in July by levying a 12.5% tax on imports from Thailand for not taking steps to oppose the use of forced labor.
Before the gala dinner Tuesday night, Trump will participate in what's billed as a "special summit" with the ASEAN leaders, where they are expected to discuss efforts to deepen trade and security ties as well as the region's longstanding conflicts, including yearslong violence in Myanmar and escalating disputes in the South China Sea, which Beijing claims virtually in its entirety.
Washington rejects China's expansive claim in the waterway, and has repeatedly stated that it's obligated to defend the Philippines if Filipino forces come under an armed attack.
Demonstrators hold signs during a protest against U.S. President Donald Trump's visit to attend the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit and related meetings in Manila, Philippines, Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026. Firdia Linsawati/AP hide caption
About 1,500 left-wing protesters held a noisy rally in a downtown Manila square ahead of Trump's arrival, calling on Philippine leaders not to take their foreign policy cues from the U.S.
They waved red flags and held up a large streamer that read, "Resist U.S. war and plunder!" They planned to burn an effigy of Trump. Riot police with shields and wooden truncheons stood nearby.
"The Philippine government should not deal with such a loser so our call to the Marcos administration is to stop being a puppet of Donald Trump and to uphold an independent foreign policy for the Philippines," protest leader Teddy Casiño told The Associated Press at the Liwasang Bonifacio square, referring to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
On Wednesday, Trump is set to receive a red-carpet welcome and full military honors from Marcos Jr., followed by a state banquet as part of his visit to the Malacanang presidential palace. Trump and Marcos are expected to affirm their commitment to their countries' longstanding treaty alliance.
Officials are arranging a possible brief reunion in Malacanang with an old acquaintance — Imelda Marcos — if she's well enough and gets her doctors' nod.
Now 97 and using a wheelchair, the former jet set Philippine first lady and mother of the incumbent president partied in New York decades ago in her heyday as the controversial wife of a strongman leader, who was to be ousted in a pro-democracy 1986 "People Power" public uprising.
But the friendship with Trump endured, with Trump often asking Marcos Jr. and other Philippine officials: "How's Imelda?" Philippine Ambassador to Washington Jose Manuel Romualdez told The Associated Press.
"Personal connections are very important to him," Romualdez said.
When the Philippine leader met Trump in the White House last year, he carried a note from his mother that thanked the U.S. president for his strong backing of the Philippines. "President Trump was very happy and told Marcos, 'please say hello to your mother,'" according to Romualdez.
Trump is also expected to announce a series of commercial deals and investments in the aviation, defense, energy, and technology sectors, before heading to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.

Blasts echoed over the Bahraini capital Manama on Tuesday, as Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they launched a drone attack, the third in five days after a weeks-long lull.
Bahrain's armed forces intercepted "Iranian aerial attacks in the kingdom's skies", according to state television, while Iran's Guards said they targeted a US-operated radar system.
Bahrain's Interior Ministry, in a post on X, warned of a "possible threat" and called on the country's residents to remain calm, move to the nearest safe place and follow only official sources for information on developments.
Bahraini officials also said the country's air defence systems had intercepted attacks from Iran.
No confirmed report has yet been released on any impact of Iranian drones on the radar system at Sheikh Isa base or on the extent of any possible damage.
The public relations arm of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps described the pre-dawn attack on Tuesday as a response to what it called "the continued violation of the airspace of the Islamic Republic of Iran" by US military drones.
It said the operation formed part of ongoing air-defence and electronic warfare measures to track, destroy and capture US drones of the MQ and MQM-170 series.
"Combat drones belonging to the Revolutionary Guards carried out a precision operation this morning, targeting a radar system operated by US forces at the Sheikh Isa Air Base in Bahrain," the Guards' Sepah news website said.
The Guards also warned that continued use of regional bases and military facilities for actions against Iran would not go unanswered.
Bahrain was heavily targeted earlier in the war, which started in February, but had been peaceful for weeks until an Iranian drone attack on Friday. A second followed on Sunday.
Friday's strike was the first Iranian attack against a Gulf country since early September.
The US military said it had shot down two drones launched Friday by Iranian forces, while the Bahraini army said it had intercepted Sunday's attack.
Bahrain, which hosts a major US naval base, has experienced numerous Iranian attacks since US-Israeli strikes on Iran triggered the Middle East war in February.
Since September, the conflict has mainly been restricted to the area around the strategic Strait of Hormuz, with the US blockading Iranian ports and Tehran attempting to control the oil shipping route.
The Middle East war will be on the agenda during an unprecedented trilateral summit between US President Donald Trump and his Chinese and Russian counterparts, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, scheduled this week in China, according to the White House.
As talks aimed at ending the war appear to be deadlocked, a third US aircraft carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, is operating in the Middle East, the US military said on Monday.

China said on Tuesday it has "no information" on whether US President Donald Trump would meet Kim Jong-un, after the US president left open the possibility of meeting the North Korean leader on his Asia trip.
"I have no information regarding this matter," foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said at a news briefing in Beijing, a day before Trump was expected in Shenzhen for an APEC meeting.
Before departing for China, Trump, who met Kim three times during his first term, left open the possibility of meeting the North Korean leader.
"We may meet with Kim Jong-un also, so that'll be good," Trump told reporters, adding that whether Kim would make the trip was "up to President Xi" of China.
As Trump made the remarks, North Korean state media reported that Kim and his family, accompanied by party officials, travelled to a tourist zone near the northern border with China on Sunday and Monday.
Photos released by the official Korean Central News Agency show Kim sitting on an armchair, grinning, with a cigarette in his hand and sunglasses on, at what appeared to be a ski resort, with his wife Ri Sol Ju standing behind him.
Another photo shows his young daughter Ju Ae, whom Seoul's spy agency has said is being groomed to be Kim's successor, skiing downhill in a white outfit but without a helmet.
The city of Samjiyon is located near the Chinese border and is close to Mount Paektu, considered by North Koreans to be the sacred birthplace of Kim's father, Jong-il.
As he toured the resort, including ski centres and hotels, Kim "expressed great satisfaction, saying that all the structures are really impeccable as they were built in a delicate way", KCNA reported.
"The more he looked at it, the more admiration he felt at the spectacular scenery reminiscent of a town in the forest," it said.
While Kim made the visit near China, which is hosting the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in the southern city of Shenzhen, experts say it was unlikely intended to signal plans to travel to the summit.
The straight-line distance between the two cities is more than 2,500 kilometres (1,553 miles).
"The KCNA report does not contain any message aimed at the United States and there are no signs of preparations for a meeting," Hong Min, a senior researcher at the Korea Institute for National Unification, told the AFP news agency.
"Kim's visit therefore is hard to be seen as a preparation for any North Korea-US meeting this week," he said.
Trump and Kim met in Singapore in June 2018, then in Hanoi in February 2019 and at the Demilitarised Zone in North Korea in June 2019.
The meetings came after Trump initially mocked Kim as "rocket man" during a speech in 2017.
The US president said in August that he expected to meet later this year with Kim, hoping to revive the bond he claims to have forged with the leader of nuclear-armed North Korea in his first term.

Camilo Rodriguez’s death comes as the country grapples with a surge in drug violence
The Costa Rican journalist Camilo Rodriguez, who gained prominence for publishing allegations against ⁠suspected drug traffickers and politicians, was shot dead on Monday, authorities said.
The first known killing of a journalist ⁠in Costa Rica in ⁠25 years, ​Rodriguez’s death comes as the country grapples with a surge in drug violence driven by international trafficking groups, despite long ⁠being regarded as one of Central America’s most peaceful and stable democracies.
Rodriguez, 51, was attacked at about 3.20pm local ⁠time amid heavy traffic on a main highway on the outskirts of the capital ​San Jose, the Red Cross ‌reported.
President Laura Fernandez condemned ‌the attack in a video message.
“I am filled with indignation and outrage over ‌the cowardly murder of communicator Camilo Rodriguez. Regardless of the content of his communications, what happened today in our country is a stain on freedom of expression,” Fernandez said.
Attorney general Carlo Diaz told local news outlet Extra Noticias that investigators found multiple bullet impacts and a crime scene resembling a contract ‌killing, likely linked to the allegations Rodriguez had published. He gave no further evidence and did not name suspects.
“We know he ​was a communicator who publicly identified people for alleged links to drug trafficking,” Diaz said, adding that Rodriguez had previously reported threats but had declined protection.
“Silencing someone who reports on drug trafficking or corruption, in this case a communicator, is a ⁠signal we cannot tolerate in a democratic society.“
Diaz pledged efforts to ​hold those responsible ​for the murder accountable.
The last such ​attack on a media worker happened in July 2001 when radio ​producer Parmenio ‌Medina was gunned ​down on a ​Santo Domingo highway, in roughly the same area as Rodriguez’s attack took place.
Costa Rica’s homicide rate doubled between 2013 and 2023 and has only eased slightly since then.

International investigation using trove of leaked internal data allegedly shows German bank overlooked compliance concerns to safeguard profits
Deutsche Bank reportedly dismissed warnings about its dealings with risky clients, including high-profile Russian oligarchs, to protect profits, the findings of an investigation into a trove of leaked bank documents indicate.
A leak of 15m internal files is reported to show that the troubled German bank repeatedly ignored concerns by its compliance officers about its risk-taking, despite having already been caught being used to launder billions of dollars for Russian criminals, spies and oligarchs between 2010 and 2015.
The investigations, which were published by media outlets including Der Spiegel, the Financial Times, the New York Times and Le Monde, will represent a fresh blow for Deutsche Bank, which has struggled to repair its reputation after a number of scandals and dealings with controversial clients including the US president, Donald Trump, and the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
Deutsche Bank said on Tuesday that the issues raised in the investigations “date back many years, in some cases as much as two decades” and had been addressed by its leadership. “Where relevant, we reviewed these matters at the time and worked closely with regulators.”
However, the reports suggested Deutsche Bank prioritised profit ahead of internal controls, and continued to expand its Russian business until 2021, despite warnings from internal compliance officers and growing geopolitical tensions between Nato allies and Moscow.
Deutsche Bank allegedly resisted pulling out of Russia even after the Kremlin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, before the bank did a U-turn and exiting the country in March that year.
The investigations suggested Deutsche Bank was driven by competitive pressure, including from American banks, and that its chief executive, Christian Sewing, pursued a growth strategy that involved doing business with a list of customers known as its “most sensitive clients”. That covered roughly 50 corporate clients ranked by how close they were to the Kremlin, and other potential risks including financial crime, according to the Financial Times.
Some names allegedly on that list included: Russia’s state-owned gas company Gazprom; petrochemicals group Sibur; and oligarchs including the aluminium magnate Oleg Deripaska, the report said.
Outside its Russian dealings, the German lender is facing fresh scrutiny for allegedly processing almost $600m (£454m) of suspicious payments linked to Epstein, much higher than previously known. Deutsche said it “regrets [its] historical relationship” with Epstein and that it had made “considerable investments in strengthening controls”.
The lender is also accused of accidentally leaking Trump’s tax documents to another client during his first term in office, which Deutsche Bank allegedly kept secret from the White House. Deutsche Bank said it did not comment on former or existing client relationships. Deutsche Bank cut ties with Trump in 2021.
The reports prompted a 4% drop in Deutsche Bank’s German-listed shares on Tuesday.
Deutsche Bank issued a public statement in response to the investigation on Tuesday, saying it had “gone through a fundamental transformation” under Sewing.
“We made substantial investments in our control environment while restoring sustainable profitability, as evidenced by record profits in 2025 as well as in recent quarters. This involved €7bn of direct investments in our control environment between 2019 and 2025.”
The bank added: “We remain committed to ensuring continuous enhancements of our control environment and a culture of integrity and completing any outstanding remediation.”
“Regardless of how the information was obtained, it includes confidential information about clients, employees and other third parties, which remains legally protected. We have acted, and will continue to act, decisively to protect this,” the bank said.

Millions of shorebirds embark on epic migrations to Alaska each year to breed. They often travel thousands of miles from places like New Zealand, Asia and South America. US President Trump said the deals would prevent ‘coercion by any single foreign supplier’.
United States President Donald Trump says that members of the Quad, a security grouping of the US and three Indo-Pacific countries, have reached agreements aimed at securing supply chains of critical minerals .
Trump met India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Australia’s Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Japan’s Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi – the other Quad leaders – in the Philippines on Thursday.
“Our countries are the four corners of a free, open, stable, and prosperous Indo-Pacific,” Trump said in remarks ahead of the meeting in Manila.
During the meeting, Trump said the agreements on critical minerals aimed to prevent “coercion by any single foreign supplier”. He did not single out China, which dominates global rare earth supplies .
Trump later said the US would have “everything we need” on rare earths in 10 months.
“We are making rare earth at a level that we’ve never made before. We’re going to catch them [China] within 10 months,” he said.
China last year imposed restrictions on exports of rare earths amid a trade dispute with the US. In June, the two sides agreed a deal aimed at restoring the US’s access to China’s rare earth supplies.
In a statement after the leaders’ meeting, the Quad expressed “grave concerns” about “economic coercion”, including through arbitrary export restrictions.
While the statement did not name any country, the US and Japan have complained about China’s restrictions on ‌exports of rare earths vital to the manufacturing of everything from electric cars to mobile phones.
China has effectively shut off exports of key critical minerals to Japan for nearly a year as relations between Asia’s two largest economies have nosedived.
It was Trump’s first meeting of the Quad grouping – which his predecessor US President Joe Biden regarded as a signature foreign policy initiative.
Scott Lucas, professor of international politics at the Clinton Institute at University College Dublin, told Al Jazeera that the meeting suggested the Quad grouping had a “functioning relationship”.
“Given the damage to the Quad during the Trump administration, including the instability caused by Trump’s tariffs on India, and India’s response by diversifying, the Quad meeting and statements like this give reassurance that there is still a functioning relationship,” Lucas said. “I’m not sure I’d call it an alliance, as I don’t think the Trump folks believe in alliances.”
Trump also joined a summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations in Manila on the first day of a three-day trip to Asia.
After the Philippines, Trump will travel to China and attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Shenzhen, where he is expected to hold a trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday.
The Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs says the talks will focus on topics of “groundbreaking significance”, including “safeguarding world peace”.
Asked by reporters about a CNN report which claimed that US intelligence had determined Tehran was developing plans to use a so-called “dirty bomb” to target officials in the Trump administration, Trump said he was “looking into it”.
He said that if Iran posed an “imminent threat” to Washington, “they will pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before”.
He added that he “hoped” Iran did not pose a threat, but that he took such a scenario “very seriously” because “they happen to be crazy”.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghei said in a post on X that “Those who initiated the aggression against Iran are now seeking to lay the media groundwork for their sinister designs by manufacturing and disseminating baseless allegations, including the recent claims published by The New York Times and the fabricated media narrative surrounding an alleged ‘dirty bomb’ propagated by CNN.”

A Costa Rican journalist who denounced alleged links between politicians and drug traffickers in the Central American country has been shot dead.
Police said gunmen on a motorbike ambushed Camilo Rodríguez, 50, as he was travelling in his car north of the capital, San José, on Monday afternoon.
The independent reporter earlier said he had been receiving death threats from drug trafficking gangs.
Local media reported that it was the first murder of a journalist in more than two decades in Costa Rica. It comes at a time when transnational crime gangs are increasing their presence in the country, driving up its formerly low homicide rate.
The president of the Costa Rican Journalists' Association, Yanancy Noguera, said that "all evidence so far points to the silencing of a dissenting voice in Costa Rica - a person who published information about organised crime in the country".
Rodríguez had been working as a journalist for several decades, both in radio and in print.
Most recently, he had been uploading videos to social media in which he named public figures such as judges, business people and politicians, which he alleged were corrupt or had ties to known drug traffickers.
In one of his videos, he alleged that the home of Costa Rica's President, Laura Fernández, had been constructed by a company that he said had links to a criminal gang.
Fernández, who categorically denied any wrongdoing, took the journalist to court, accusing him of defamation.
Reacting to his murder in a video message, the president strongly condemned the attack, calling it "a stain on freedom of expression".
She added that she had instructed police to do their utmost to "punish Camilo's murderers".
Rodríguez had also tried to stand for political office, seeking to run as the presidential candidate for the Costa Rican Renovation Party in 2021.
However, his candidacy was rejected by the electoral authorities after the party failed to meet the necessary criteria required to file candidates.
Costa Rica's Attorney General, Carlo Díaz, said that "silencing someone who reports on drug trafficking or corruption, in this case a communicator, is a signal we cannot tolerate in a democratic society".
Candidate tough on crime wins Costa Rica presidential election
